topics.why: This closes the GD bank on a genuinely open, forward-looking debate rather than a settled policy question, fitting for the sector's early-stage nature.
topics.starter: Strip away the green bonds, the concessional loans and the PLI incentives - would India's climate-tech startups actually survive on their own unit economics?
points_for: Falling renewable-energy and storage costs are making some climate-tech business models genuinely competitive on unit economics alone, not just policy support.
Early-stage 2026 funding data specifically flags climate-tech (alongside AI and D2C) as an area seeing more deal activity - a sign investors see a path to standalone viability emerging.

Mandatory ESG reporting for large listed companies indirectly creates commercial demand for climate-tech B2B services like emissions tracking and green-loan structuring - a subsidy-independent revenue driver.

Asset-light categories like carbon accounting SaaS, energy-management software and climate-risk analytics have cost structures closer to normal enterprise software than to capital-intensive clean-energy hardware, making them commercially self-sustaining sooner.
points_against: Much of India's climate-tech ecosystem still relies on green bonds, concessional financing or PLI-style incentives to reach commercial scale.

Hardware-heavy categories like battery storage, clean-energy generation and EV charging infrastructure carry capital costs that are still difficult to recover without policy support or subsidised financing.

Corporate demand for climate-tech services is itself partly a function of regulation like BRSR and carbon markets rather than pure market pull, meaning the 'subsidy' is often just one step removed rather than absent.

Climate-tech's long payback periods and technology risk make private capital more expensive and harder to raise than for conventional startups, keeping many founders reliant on blended or concessional funding.
'Fully commercially viable without any subsidy' remains true for only a subset of climate-tech categories today, like carbon accounting SaaS, more than others, like hardware-heavy clean energy.

latest.text: Early-stage Indian startup funding in FY2026 saw more deal activity specifically in AI, climate-tech and D2C brands, even as later-stage funding stayed more selective.

topics.title: Faith-tech and spiritual commerce: genuine cultural business, or exploiting belief for profit?
topics.hook: Faith-tech and spiritual-commerce startups - astrology-based remedies delivered through a modern startup structure - are a genuinely distinctive, India-specific business category.
topics.why: This is a genuinely distinctive, India-specific startup category worth debating directly, distinct from the climate-tech and ESG-focused startup niche covered elsewhere.
topics.starter: Millions of Indians already consult an astrologer without a second thought - so is putting that in an app just modernising a cultural practice, or professionalising something that works precisely because it isn't held to the standards we'd apply to, say, financial advice?
points_for: Astrology and spiritual guidance have deep, longstanding cultural roots in India - a startup professionalising and improving access to this isn't inherently exploitative.

Bringing structured, tech-enabled delivery to a previously informal, unregulated market can actually improve consistency and reduce the risk of outright fraud compared to unverified local practitioners.

Consumers are voluntarily choosing to pay for a service that has existed in Indian society for centuries in one form or another; treating it differently from other belief-adjacent services like wellness or life coaching is arguably inconsistent.
As with any consumer category, market competition and reviews create some natural accountability pressure on providers to deliver a service customers find genuinely valuable.
points_against: Startups built on belief-based products can create real financial and emotional pressure on vulnerable customers seeking guidance during difficult life moments.
Unlike pharma or financial advice, spiritual/astrology-based commerce faces very little consumer-protection-specific regulation in India today.
The subscription and repeat-purchase models common to app-based platforms can be designed to maximise engagement and spend in ways that exploit anxiety rather than genuinely help customers.
The cross-functional 'founder's office' structure typical of early-stage startups here suggests a company still defining its own ethical and operational playbook, not an established, scrutinised one.

Without standardised qualifications for who can offer paid spiritual guidance, quality and intent vary enormously across providers on the same platform, unlike more credentialed professional-services categories.

topics.title: Healthcare-and-staffing business transformation: can 'operational excellence' language mask real workforce precarity?
topics.hook: Healthcare-and-staffing businesses increasingly frame their strategy around 'business transformation' and 'operational excellence' - language worth interrogating given staffing-industry labour dynamics.
topics.why: This connects the sector's strategy-consulting themes to the Labour Codes and gig-worker-protection debates running through HR and Operations more broadly.
topics.starter: Every staffing company today talks about 'operational excellence' - but when the workforce being optimised is healthcare staff, is that efficiency, or just a nicer word for precarity?
points_for: Healthcare staffing genuinely benefits from better operational matching - right skills, right shift, right location - real efficiency gains that help both providers and staff.
Technology-driven scheduling and matching can reduce chronic understaffing and burnout in healthcare settings, a genuine patient-safety and worker-wellbeing win.
Better operational systems can create more predictable, transparent shift allocation for workers, replacing opaque, manual assignment processes that often favoured insiders.
Efficiency gains that reduce a staffing firm's costs can, in a competitive labour market, translate into better pay and benefits to attract and retain scarce healthcare talent.
points_against: 'Operational excellence' in staffing businesses can sometimes mean optimising for lower-cost, less secure contract labour rather than genuine service improvement.

India's 2026 Labour Codes' new protections for contract and fixed-term workers directly affect how healthcare-staffing businesses can structure their workforce going forward, suggesting regulators see a real risk here.

'Transformation' language is easy to apply retroactively to justify workforce cuts or reclassification of employees as contractors, making the framing hard to distinguish from cost-cutting without seeing the actual numbers.

Healthcare staffing specifically involves life-and-safety stakes, so precarity in this sector - rushed shifts, understaffing, inexperienced substitutes - carries higher real-world costs than in most other gig-economy contexts.

The honest answer likely depends entirely on execution - the same 'transformation' language can describe genuinely better matching or thinly-disguised cost-cutting, and it's worth asking which a specific company means.

latest.text: India's Labour Codes introduce stronger protections for fixed-term and contract employees (including pro-rata gratuity), directly affecting how staffing-heavy healthcare businesses can structure their workforce.

topics.title: Should India adopt a Uniform Civil Code nationally, not state by state?
topics.hook: Four states have passed their own UCC laws in the last two years - Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh - with Rajasthan actively drafting its own.
topics.why: A genuinely live, fast-moving constitutional and social debate - several states have moved in 2026 alone, making this a strong, current GD topic beyond textbook framing.
topics.starter: Four states have already passed their own version of a Uniform Civil Code in the last two years - so is a national UCC now inevitable, or does state-by-state adoption prove we don't actually need one law for the whole country?
points_for: Article 44 of the Constitution explicitly directs the state toward a uniform civil code, and a single national law would end the current patchwork of differing state rules.
A national law would give every citizen the same civil rights regardless of which state they live in, rather than rights depending on geography.

Common threads already converging across passed state laws - mandatory marriage/live-in registration, monogamy, expanded divorce grounds for women - suggest genuine common ground exists to build a national consensus on.
A single national framework would reduce the legal complexity and forum-shopping risk that arises when personal-law questions can be litigated differently depending on the state a case arises in.
points_against: Critics argue a rushed, majoritarian-driven UCC risks imposing one community's civil norms on religious and cultural minorities rather than genuinely harmonising personal law.
A state-led patchwork, while imperfect, allows differing regional social contexts and political consensus levels to be respected rather than forcing one national timeline on all states at once.

Four states passing UCC laws in two years already creates confusing, inconsistent rights depending on where a citizen lives - is that a pragmatic path to eventual national consensus, or a problem in itself?

Genuine implementation of a national UCC would require reconciling deeply varied personal-law traditions across multiple religions, tribal customary law and regional practices, a far more complex undertaking than any single state's version has yet attempted.
Rushing a national law before state-level experiments mature risks locking in early, potentially flawed provisions before better practices have had a chance to emerge from state-level experience.

latest.text: Madhya Pradesh passed its own UCC Bill on 21 July 2026, becoming the fourth state (fifth counting Goa's historic code) to adopt one, with Rajasthan's expert panel actively drafting a fifth.
Assam passed its UCC Bill, becoming the first north-eastern state to do so, alongside Uttarakhand (2024) and Gujarat (March 2026).

topics.title: Is 'One Nation, One Election' good for Indian democracy?
topics.hook: A Joint Parliamentary Committee has now had its deadline extended multiple times through 2026 while it scrutinises the constitutional amendment needed for simultaneous polls.
topics.why: A structurally significant electoral-reform debate that's been actively moving through Parliament in 2026, not a settled or purely hypothetical question.
topics.starter: Frequent elections cost money and freeze governance under the model code of conduct - but is fixing that worth the risk of one national wave drowning out every state's own issues?
points_for: Frequent state and national elections disrupt governance through model code of conduct freezes and impose massive recurring costs - synchronising polls could free up governance bandwidth and money.
Perpetual campaign mode across staggered elections diverts political leaders' and bureaucrats' attention from long-term policy execution toward continuous electioneering.
Countries like South Africa and Sweden do run simultaneous elections successfully, showing the model is not inherently unworkable, even if scale differs.
A synchronised calendar could reduce voter fatigue and potentially improve overall turnout by consolidating civic engagement into fewer, higher-salience election events.
points_against: Critics argue it structurally advantages whichever party has national momentum at the shared election moment, potentially drowning out distinct state-level issues and reducing federal accountability.

Aligning Lok Sabha and all state assembly terms requires genuinely difficult constitutional amendments (Articles 83, 85, 172, 174) and has no easy transition path for states with differently-timed terms.

If a state government falls mid-term under a synchronised system, the fix - President's Rule or a short 'unexpired term' assembly - creates its own governance instability that staggered elections don't have.
India's scale and federal, linguistic diversity is nowhere close to the countries cited as successful examples of simultaneous elections, making direct comparisons weak evidence either way.
Parliament's Joint Committee needing repeated deadline extensions through 2026 itself suggests the practical and legal complexity is proving harder to resolve than proponents initially argued.

latest.text: Parliament's Joint Committee on the ONOE bills was granted a further extension to submit its report, continuing a pattern of repeated deadline extensions through 2025-26.

topics.title: Should India finally pass a dedicated cryptocurrency law?
topics.hook: India has one of the world's largest crypto markets (~39 million investors, ~$2.1 billion held) - and still no dedicated law, just a tax-and-tolerate regime built on income-tax classification.
topics.why: A genuinely unresolved, actively-debated regulatory gap, with the RBI reportedly hardening its stance even as a new framework is discussed ahead of the Union Budget.
topics.starter: India has roughly 39 million crypto investors and still no dedicated law - just a 30% tax that experts say is pushing trading offshore - so is 'tax and tolerate' actually a policy, or just an excuse to avoid deciding?
points_for: Legal clarity - defined asset classes, licensing, multi-regulator roles for SEBI/RBI - would reduce the current ambiguity that pushes both investors and platforms into a grey zone.

A flat 30% tax plus 1% TDS is widely blamed for pushing liquidity to offshore, harder-to-regulate platforms rather than achieving its intended oversight - a clearer law could fix that incentive problem directly.
Prolonged ambiguity risks pushing crypto talent and startups to more clearly-regulated jurisdictions like the UAE or Singapore, a real opportunity cost even for those skeptical of crypto itself.
With roughly 39 million Indian investors already holding crypto assets, treating the market as effectively unregulated leaves a large number of retail investors without clear consumer protections.
points_against: RBI's own internal position reportedly leans toward prohibition, reflecting genuine concern about financial-stability risk and monitoring difficulty for overseas-exchange trading.
Legitimising crypto through a dedicated regulatory framework could be read as an implicit endorsement that encourages further retail speculation in a volatile asset class.
Cryptocurrencies operating outside India's monetary system complicate capital-account management and could undermine the rupee's role in domestic transactions if adoption grows unchecked.

Coordinating a workable framework across SEBI, RBI and the Finance Ministry, each with different mandates and risk tolerances, has proven difficult for years, suggesting caution may reflect genuine unresolved disagreement rather than mere inertia.

latest.text: Reuters reported that internal government documents show the RBI's position hardening toward prohibition, even as the Finance Ministry discusses a new regulatory framework with SEBI ahead of the Union Budget.

topics.title: Should social media platforms be held legally responsible for user-generated content?
topics.hook: As AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation scale faster than moderation can catch them, the 'platform vs. publisher' legal question has become urgent rather than academic.
topics.why: A foundational tech-policy debate directly relevant to any student heading into a marketing, media or tech career, where content moderation increasingly shapes what's even possible to publish.
topics.starter: When an algorithm decides what a billion people see next, is that platform still just hosting content - or has it effectively become the publisher?
points_for: Platforms actively shape what users see through recommendation algorithms - real editorial influence that arguably comes with real editorial responsibility.
AI-generated deepfake and synthetic-media content blurs the line between 'user-generated' and 'platform-generated' content in ways that make platforms' role look more active, not more passive.
Without meaningful liability, platforms have limited commercial incentive to invest seriously in moderation and safety systems beyond the legal minimum.

ASCI's 2026 rules already extend disclosure obligations to AI-generated virtual influencers, showing regulators believe platforms and advertisers can reasonably be held to specific content-related standards.
points_against: Making platforms legally liable for user content at scale could push them toward excessive, over-cautious content removal, chilling legitimate speech.

India's current framework of IT Rules and safe-harbour provisions already sits in between - conditional immunity that depends on platforms complying with takedown and due-diligence obligations, rather than a binary liable/not-liable choice.
Holding platforms fully liable for the sheer volume of content posted every second is practically unworkable without either automated over-blocking or an enormous, costly human-moderation apparatus.
Broad liability could raise compliance costs enough to entrench dominant incumbents further, since only the largest platforms could afford the legal and moderation infrastructure required.

Deepfake and synthetic-media harms may be better addressed through targeted rules on specific harmful content categories than through a blanket liability standard applied to all user-generated content.

latest.text: ASCI's 2026 rules specifically extended disclosure and monitoring requirements to AI-generated virtual influencers, reflecting how regulators are already treating AI content as a distinct compliance category.

topics.title: Is the 4-day work week a genuine benefit, or repackaged overwork?
topics.hook: India's new Labour Codes now legally permit a 4-day week - but only by compressing the same 48 hours into four 12-hour days, not by cutting total hours.
topics.why: A workplace-policy debate that just became concretely real in India, not a hypothetical imported from Western trials - highly relevant to every student about to enter the workforce.
topics.starter: India's Labour Codes now legally allow a four-day week - but it's the same 48 hours squeezed into four 12-hour days, so is that actually rest, or just overwork wearing a better outfit?
points_for: Three consecutive days off genuinely improves recovery and personal-life bandwidth compared to the standard two-day weekend, especially for output-measured (not time-measured) knowledge work.
It's opt-in, not mandatory - meaning it can be adopted precisely where it makes sense, without being forced onto contexts where it doesn't.
Experts expect IT, consulting and knowledge-work sectors to adopt this fastest, since those roles can most easily reorganise output around fewer, more focused days.
Fewer commuting days and a longer contiguous break can measurably reduce burnout and improve retention in competitive, talent-scarce sectors.
points_against: Critics point out this isn't a shorter work week at all - just a repackaging into fewer, longer, more exhausting days, with real burnout risk in 12-hour shifts.

Because employees must agree and employers can't impose it unilaterally, real-world impact depends heavily on individual company culture and negotiating power - workers with less leverage may face pressure to 'agree' regardless.
Sectors like healthcare, manufacturing and logistics face real operational barriers to compressed scheduling, meaning any benefit is unevenly available across India's workforce.
Twelve-hour shifts raise genuine safety and cognitive-fatigue concerns in roles requiring sustained attention or physical labour, unlike desk-based knowledge work.
Without total weekly hours actually falling, the model does little to address the underlying overwork problem - it just redistributes the same hours differently.

latest.text: India's Labour Codes rules formally enabled a legally optional 4-day work week (with 12-hour shifts) as part of the broader 2026 labour-law overhaul, requiring mutual employer-employee agreement.

topics.title: Should India seriously consider a Universal Basic Income?
topics.hook: As AI reshapes entry-level hiring across IT, finance and professional services, UBI has moved from a fringe economic idea to a mainstream policy question globally.
topics.why: This connects directly to the AI-and-jobs disruption already reshaping India's white-collar hiring market - a policy response worth debating on its own economic merits.
topics.starter: As AI eats into entry-level hiring, is a basic income the safety net India needs to build now, or a fiscal commitment the country simply can't afford yet?
points_for: As AI-driven job displacement grows, with entry-level tech hiring already down meaningfully, an income floor could cushion the transition without discouraging work entirely, unlike some traditional welfare designs.
India already runs large direct-benefit-transfer infrastructure that is Aadhaar-linked and UPI-enabled, which would make implementation more technically feasible here than in many other countries.
A simple, universal cash transfer reduces the administrative overhead and leakage historically associated with India's many overlapping, means-tested welfare schemes.
Direct cash gives recipients autonomy to spend on their actual priorities - education, healthcare, small business capital - rather than the government pre-deciding through in-kind schemes.
points_against: India's fiscal capacity is already stretched, and a truly meaningful UBI at national scale would require either steep tax increases or cuts to existing targeted welfare programs.
Universal versus targeted design profoundly changes both the cost and the political feasibility of any scheme - a genuinely universal UBI at meaningful levels may simply be unaffordable.
Cash transfers alone don't address structural gaps like healthcare access or skilling infrastructure that in-kind and targeted programs are specifically designed to fill.
Inflationary effects of a large, recurring cash injection into the economy are hard to predict at India's population scale, and could erode the very purchasing power UBI is meant to protect.
The debate is really about willingness to fund it, not capability to deliver it - meaning the harder question is a political and fiscal trade-off, not a technical one.

latest.text: AI-linked entry-level hiring disruption (freshers now just 13% of active tech openings) is renewing global and Indian policy debate about income-support responses to structural, AI-driven job displacement.

topics.title: Should India privatize more public sector undertakings?
topics.hook: India's PSU divestment pace has been uneven for years, even as GCCs and private capital increasingly outcompete public enterprises for talent and capital efficiency.
topics.why: A perennial economic-policy GD staple, still genuinely contested and directly relevant to India's ongoing growth and jobs debate.
topics.starter: Every year the government talks about disinvestment, and every year the pace stays uneven - so is India actually committed to privatizing its PSUs, or just committed to talking about it?
points_for: Private ownership generally improves capital efficiency and reduces the fiscal burden of loss-making PSUs, freeing government resources for other priorities like infrastructure and welfare.
GCCs and private capital increasingly outcompete public enterprises for talent and capital efficiency, suggesting PSUs risk becoming structurally uncompetitive if left unreformed.
Privatisation proceeds can be redirected toward capital-intensive public priorities rather than propping up underperforming assets indefinitely.
Reduced political interference in day-to-day operations under private ownership can improve decision-making speed and accountability compared to bureaucratic PSU governance structures.
points_against: PSUs in strategic sectors like defence, energy and banking carry national-security and public-service considerations that a pure efficiency lens doesn't fully capture.
PSU privatization has historically triggered genuine workforce anxiety and resistance - any serious push needs a credible transition plan for existing employees, not just a sale.
Some PSUs serve social and developmental mandates like rural banking access or subsidised essential services that a profit-maximising private owner would have little incentive to continue.

India's actual practiced approach has increasingly been targeted disinvestment in non-strategic sectors while retaining control of a smaller set of core PSUs, suggesting even policymakers see full-scale privatisation as neither necessary nor desirable.

Poorly executed privatisation - underpriced asset sales, weak regulatory oversight of the new private owner - can transfer public value to private hands without delivering the promised efficiency gains.

topics.title: Is India's demographic dividend turning into a jobless-growth problem?
topics.hook: India's median age of 27 is often cited as a structural growth advantage - but AI-driven hiring shifts are raising real questions about whether enough jobs exist to capture it.
topics.why: This ties India's most-cited long-term economic advantage directly to the very current AI-and-jobs disruption already reshaping India's hiring landscape.
topics.starter: India's median age is 27 - the number everyone cites as our biggest growth advantage - but if AI keeps eating entry-level hiring, are we actually capturing that dividend, or just aging into a jobs shortfall?
points_for: India's overall hiring grew 15% YoY into 2026, and GCC/AI-linked roles are expanding fast enough to still represent a genuine structural opportunity.
India's Skills Report 2026 shows national employability rising to 56.3%, suggesting the workforce is becoming more job-ready even as the job mix shifts.

India remains one of the few large economies with a growing working-age population precisely when many developed economies face shrinking labour forces, a structural advantage that doesn't disappear even if entry-level hiring softens temporarily.

New sectors like GCCs, deep-tech, climate-tech and space are creating categories of jobs that didn't exist a decade ago, showing the economy is still generating fresh demand even as older job categories shift.
points_against: Entry-level, degree-dependent white-collar hiring specifically has weakened even as GDP and senior hiring both grow - a genuine mismatch between demographic supply and entry-level demand.

Freshers now make up just 13% of active tech job openings, a sharp reduction from historical norms, indicating AI-driven automation of entry-level tasks is a specific, current phenomenon and not just a cyclical dip.
GCC and tech-linked job growth concentrates heavily in a handful of metro and tier-2 hubs, leaving the dividend argument much weaker for large parts of the country outside those clusters.

The debate increasingly isn't about the number of jobs, but whether India's education system is producing the specific, AI-era skills employers now demand - a skills mismatch that raw hiring-growth numbers can mask.

A demographic dividend requires jobs at the pace of population entering the workforce every year; even solid percentage hiring growth may not be enough in absolute terms given India's sheer cohort size.

latest.text: India's Skills Report 2026 shows national employability rising to 56.3%, even as freshers fell to just 13% of active tech job openings - a genuine tension between rising skills and shrinking entry-level absorption.

topics.title: Will Artificial General Intelligence arrive within this decade - and should that worry us?
topics.hook: Agentic AI spending is projected to more than double in 2026 alone, with leading labs and investors treating AGI timelines as a near-term planning question, not science fiction.
topics.why: A genuinely current frontier-technology debate that connects directly to the AI-jobs disruption already central to several sectors of India's economy.
topics.starter: Agentic AI spending is set to more than double this year alone - so is AGI a near-term planning question the way leading labs treat it, or still science fiction dressed up in a market forecast?
points_for: The pace of capability jumps in reasoning, multi-step planning and tool use over the past two years has consistently outpaced most public predictions from just a few years earlier.
Gartner projects global agentic AI spending will reach $201.9 billion in 2026, a 141% increase over 2025, reflecting how rapidly autonomous AI capability is scaling in practice, not just research.

Even short of 'true AGI,' the economic and labour-market disruption from increasingly capable, increasingly autonomous AI systems is already measurable and accelerating - arguably the more practically important question anyway.

Leading AI labs and major investors are explicitly planning around near-term AGI-level timelines in their own strategy and capital allocation, which is itself meaningful evidence about where informed insiders think this is heading.
points_against: Many researchers argue today's models still lack genuine reasoning and world-modelling capability, and scaling current architectures further may hit diminishing returns before reaching anything like general intelligence.
Impressive benchmark performance doesn't always translate to reliable, generalisable real-world capability - many AI systems still fail unpredictably outside their training distribution.

Predictions of imminent transformative AI have repeatedly been wrong in AI's history, with earlier AI winters following similar hype cycles, which should make forecasters cautious about extrapolating recent progress in a straight line.

India's own AI ecosystem shows an adoption-governance gap, with 74% exploring agentic AI but only around 23% having mature governance - a sign that even current, narrower AI capability is outpacing organisations' ability to responsibly deploy it, independent of whether true AGI ever arrives.
Defining 'AGI' itself remains genuinely contested among experts, making any specific decade-scale prediction hard to falsify or verify either way.

latest.text: Gartner projects global agentic AI spending will reach $201.9 billion in 2026 - a 141% increase over 2025 - reflecting how rapidly autonomous AI capability is scaling in practice, not just in research.

topics.title: Should AI-generated content require mandatory watermarking by law?
topics.hook: ASCI already mandates disclosure for AI-generated virtual influencers in India - a preview of where broader AI-content labelling law could head.
topics.why: A concrete, fast-moving regulatory question directly connected to marketing and analytics roles, where AI-generated content is already a daily reality.
topics.starter: If a fake video can be indistinguishable from a real one within seconds of being generated, is a watermark law actually protecting the public, or just giving everyone a false sense that it is?
points_for: As AI-generated images, video and audio become indistinguishable from real content, some technical labelling standard is arguably necessary to preserve basic public trust in media.
ASCI's 2026 rules already require explicit disclosure for AI-generated virtual influencers in advertising - a narrower, working example showing a mandate can be implemented in at least one sector.
Even an imperfect watermark raises the cost and reduces the scale of malicious deepfake campaigns, functioning as a meaningful deterrent even if not a perfect solution.

A legal watermarking requirement creates clear liability for platforms and creators who deliberately strip or fake disclosure, giving regulators and courts a concrete standard to enforce against, unlike today's ambiguity.
points_against: Watermarking is technically circumventable, since crops, re-encoding and screenshots strip most current watermarks, so a legal mandate may create a false sense of security without solving the underlying problem.
Detecting and penalising violations at internet scale remains a genuinely unsolved technical and regulatory challenge globally, not just in India, making enforcement largely aspirational.
A patchwork of national watermarking standards without global interoperability lets bad actors simply generate or host content in jurisdictions without the requirement.
Mandating watermarks for legitimate AI tools does little against sophisticated actors who would use unregulated, open-source, or overseas tools specifically to avoid the requirement.
Compliance costs could fall disproportionately on smaller creators and platforms, while large, well-resourced bad actors have the technical means to work around the mandate anyway.

latest.text: ASCI tightened rules on AI-generated virtual influencers amid a broader government crackdown on deepfake advertising, a working precedent for mandatory AI-content disclosure.

topics.title: Is social media doing more harm than good to youth mental health?
topics.hook: This debate has moved from parental anecdote to hard policy question globally, as several countries actively legislate age limits and platform design rules for minors.
topics.why: A perennial, high-stakes GD topic with direct relevance to the marketing and content-creation careers many of this batch's students are entering.
topics.starter: Ask any teenager whether social media makes them feel worse and most will say yes - so why is the actual research on whether it causes that harm still so contested?
points_for: A substantial and growing body of research links heavy social media use to anxiety, disrupted sleep and social-comparison-driven self-esteem issues in adolescents specifically.

Engagement-maximising design choices like infinite scroll, algorithmic feeds and push notifications are deliberately built to capture attention in ways that can override a young user's own self-regulation.
Several countries are now actively legislating age limits and platform design rules for minors, a policy response that reflects a growing global consensus that the risk is serious enough to act on.
Peer-comparison dynamics are structurally amplified on social platforms in a way earlier generations' media environments never replicated at the same scale or intensity.
points_against: Correlation between social media use and poor mental health doesn't cleanly prove causation - the platforms may also provide genuine community and support for isolated or marginalised youth.

Critics increasingly separate the harm from 'social media use itself' versus 'specific engagement-maximising design choices' - a distinction that changes what regulation should actually target, rather than banning the medium outright.
For LGBTQ+, rural, or otherwise isolated youth, social platforms can be a primary source of community and information unavailable to them offline, complicating a blanket 'net harm' verdict.

Broader social and economic stressors like academic pressure, job-market anxiety and family dynamics are confounding factors that make isolating social media's specific contribution to youth mental health difficult to establish with confidence.

For marketing and content-creation-track students specifically, this raises a genuine professional-ethics question about the techniques they may be asked to deploy for engagement - worth raising directly rather than treating this as purely someone else's policy problem.

topics.title: Is remote work a permanent shift, or has the return-to-office won?
topics.hook: Even as India's Labour Codes formally enable flexible scheduling like the 4-day week, many large employers have simultaneously pushed harder for in-office presence through 2025-26.
topics.why: A direct, personal question for every student in this batch about to enter the workforce and negotiate their own work arrangement.
topics.starter: Is remote work still winning the argument, or have we just been slow to notice that return-to-office already quietly won?
points_for: Many roles, especially in IT, consulting and knowledge work, have demonstrated sustained productivity without full-time office presence, and talent increasingly treats flexibility as a genuine expectation, not a perk.
India's Labour Codes formally enabling flexible scheduling like the 4-day week signals that policy itself is moving toward accommodating more flexible work arrangements, not away from them.
Remote and hybrid arrangements expand the effective talent pool companies can hire from beyond commutable distance to a physical office, a real competitive advantage in tight talent markets.
Cost savings on real estate and overhead give employers their own independent incentive to sustain at least partial remote arrangements, separate from employee preference.
points_against: Several large employers globally and in India have reversed earlier remote-first policies, citing collaboration, mentorship and culture-building as harder to replicate remotely, especially for early-career employees.

Some research suggests junior employees specifically benefit more from in-person mentorship and informal learning than more senior employees do - a genuine nuance that argues against a one-size-fits-all remote policy.

Even as flexible scheduling gets legally enabled, many large employers have simultaneously pushed harder for in-office presence through 2025-26, suggesting policy permission and employer practice are moving in different directions.
Full remote and full in-office are both becoming less common than negotiated hybrid arrangements, which arguably means neither side of this debate's extreme position has actually 'won.'
Measuring genuine productivity loss or gain from remote work is difficult and contested, making company RTO decisions as much about management preference and control as about proven output data.

topics.title: Should India bet bigger on nuclear energy to meet its climate goals?
topics.hook: As India's renewable buildout accelerates, nuclear remains a comparatively small but increasingly debated part of the country's clean-energy mix.
topics.why: A genuine energy-policy trade-off question, relevant to sustainability-track students and increasingly to any business operating under mandatory ESG/BRSR disclosure.
topics.starter: Solar and wind get all the attention in India's clean-energy story - but can they actually replace the steady baseload power that only nuclear reliably delivers?
points_for: Nuclear offers reliable, low-carbon baseload power that solar and wind, being intermittent, can't fully replace without matching large-scale storage investment.
The government has set ambitious nuclear-capacity targets alongside its renewables push, treating the two as complementary rather than competing priorities - a signal of genuine policy commitment.
Nuclear's small land and material footprint per unit of power generated makes it attractive for a land-constrained, densely populated country trying to scale clean baseload capacity.

As mandatory ESG reporting expands, energy-mix credibility - including views on nuclear - increasingly becomes a disclosed, scrutinised corporate position, giving large power consumers a real incentive to back reliable low-carbon sources.
points_against: Nuclear plants carry high upfront capital costs, long construction timelines, and unresolved public concerns about safety and waste - renewables remain faster and cheaper to deploy at scale today.

India's civil nuclear liability law and land-acquisition challenges have historically slowed project timelines well beyond initial targets, raising doubts about how fast capacity can realistically scale.
Renewable-plus-storage costs continue to fall rapidly, narrowing the reliability gap that nuclear's baseload argument depends on.
Public and political resistance to nuclear siting remains a real, non-technical barrier that can delay projects regardless of the economic case.

Capital committed to a single large nuclear plant takes years to generate any power at all, whereas the same capital spread across distributed renewable and storage projects can start delivering clean energy incrementally and sooner.

topics.title: Are EVs genuinely greener than ICE vehicles in India's current energy mix?
topics.hook: India's EV sales crossed record monthly highs through 2026 even as a large share of the country's electricity generation still comes from coal.
topics.why: A frequently-cited but rarely-interrogated claim - a strong critical-thinking GD topic given how fast EV adoption is scaling in India right now.
topics.starter: India just posted record EV sales growth while still running its grid largely on coal - so are these cars actually greener today, or just greener on a spreadsheet that assumes the grid catches up?
points_for: Even accounting for coal-heavy grid electricity, EVs typically produce lower lifecycle emissions than comparable ICE vehicles due to far higher powertrain efficiency.
GST on EVs was cut from 12% to 5%, alongside state-level incentives like Delhi's 2026 EV policy, reflecting a clear government bet that the net environmental case favours EVs even now.

EVs' environmental advantage strengthens every year as the grid adds more renewable capacity, meaning today's numbers already understate the lifetime benefit for vehicles that will run for a decade or more.
EVs eliminate tailpipe emissions entirely at the point of use, providing an immediate local air-quality benefit in congested Indian cities regardless of how the underlying grid is generated.
points_against: Battery manufacturing, including mining and energy-intensive production, carries a real upfront carbon cost that needs enough clean-driving mileage to offset - genuinely dependent on India's grid mix improving over the vehicle's life.

A large share of India's electricity generation still comes from coal, meaning an EV charged predominantly off a coal-heavy grid captures a smaller share of its theoretical lifecycle advantage than the same vehicle would in a cleaner-grid country.
Battery disposal and recycling infrastructure in India is still immature, creating a genuine end-of-life environmental question that the 'EVs are greener' framing often glosses over.

Mineral extraction for batteries - lithium, cobalt, nickel - carries its own significant environmental and social costs, often concentrated in countries with weaker environmental regulation than where the EVs are ultimately sold.

The debate is really about how much credit to give a trajectory versus today's exact numbers - a fair skeptic can grant that EVs will clearly be greener eventually while still questioning claims about today's grid-adjusted reality.

latest.text: India's EV sales reached 3,07,752 units in July 2026 alone (up 63% YoY), while Delhi's new EV Policy 2026 offered full road-tax and registration exemptions to accelerate adoption further.

topics.title: Is India's urban water crisis a bigger near-term threat than climate change itself?
topics.hook: Major Indian cities have faced recurring, severe water-stress episodes even as national climate policy debate focuses heavily on longer-term emissions targets.
topics.why: A useful reframing GD topic that forces a comparison between a slower-moving global threat and an acute, immediate local one.
topics.starter: Climate change gets all the long-term policy attention - but when a city literally runs short of water this summer, is that not the more urgent crisis sitting right in front of us?
points_for: Unlike climate change's longer time horizon, several Indian cities already face acute, near-term water-supply crises directly affecting daily life and economic activity.

A severe monsoon deficit in June 2026, 46% below normal in parts of the country, already measurably hit FMCG demand and rural incomes - a concrete, current illustration of the stakes, not a distant projection.

Water is a state subject in India's federal structure, creating coordination challenges that national climate policy doesn't face in the same way, making the crisis harder to address quickly through central action alone.
Urban water stress directly threatens public health through contamination and waterborne disease risk during shortages, in ways that are immediate rather than playing out over decades.
points_against: Erratic monsoons and groundwater depletion are themselves climate-linked - the water crisis is arguably a leading symptom of climate change, not a separate problem competing for attention.
Treating them as competing threats risks under-investing in the root-cause climate mitigation that would also reduce future water stress, rather than only managing symptoms.

Climate change drives other slow-building risks like heat stress, agricultural yield decline and coastal sea-level rise that are just as consequential as water stress but easier to underrate precisely because they're less immediately visible.

Long-term climate policy and near-term water management aren't mutually exclusive priorities - framing this as an either/or choice may itself be a false dichotomy that weakens the case for sustained investment in both.

Solving water-crisis symptoms through tankers, desalination or river interlinking without addressing the climate drivers behind erratic rainfall only buys time rather than fixing the underlying problem.

latest.text: India recorded a 46% rainfall deficit in parts of June 2026, one of the driest such periods in over a century, with measurable knock-on effects on rural incomes and consumption.

topics.title: Should India prioritize economic growth over environmental protection?
topics.hook: A GD classic, freshly relevant as GST 2.0 stimulates consumption-led growth even while mandatory ESG/BRSR reporting simultaneously tightens on corporate India.
topics.why: A foundational, evergreen policy trade-off - worth including precisely because it remains genuinely contested and rewards structured, balanced argument.
topics.starter: With hundreds of millions of Indians still climbing out of poverty, is it fair to ask this generation to slow growth down for environmental goals that wealthier countries never accepted on their own way up?
points_for: With hundreds of millions still climbing out of poverty, near-term economic growth arguably has the largest, most direct impact on quality of life for the most people.

Historically, developed nations grew first and cleaned up later; expecting India to forgo growth for environmental purity that wealthier nations never accepted during their own development is a real fairness concern.

Growth generates the fiscal capacity, through tax revenue and private investment, that ultimately funds environmental protection and clean-technology adoption, making growth a prerequisite for environmental spending, not a competitor to it.

GST 2.0's consumption-led stimulus shows policymakers actively prioritising near-term growth momentum even while other simultaneous measures address environmental concerns, suggesting growth-first needn't mean environment-never.
points_against: Environmental damage such as water stress, air quality and climate volatility increasingly imposes direct, measurable economic costs of its own - growth and environment aren't cleanly separable choices.

Air pollution alone imposes significant healthcare costs and productivity losses in Indian cities, meaning growth-first policies that ignore environmental cost may be self-defeating even on pure economic terms.

Locking in carbon-intensive infrastructure now, like coal plants and fossil-fuel vehicle fleets, creates costly stranded-asset risk later as global markets and regulations shift toward decarbonisation.

Mandatory ESG/BRSR reporting and GST-linked EV incentives both reflect an attempt to align growth and environmental goals rather than trade one off against the other, suggesting policymakers themselves increasingly reject a strict either/or framing.
Even with 'green growth' framing, genuine trade-offs still exist at the margin - a strong answer should acknowledge this rather than claim the tension has been fully resolved.

topics.title: Is India's National Education Policy actually being implemented, or stuck on paper?
topics.hook: Years after NEP 2020's approval, implementation quality varies enormously by state and institution - a genuine gap between policy ambition and ground reality.
topics.why: Directly relevant to this batch's own educational journey and to the education-consulting and edtech themes covered elsewhere in this GD bank.
topics.starter: NEP 2020 promised to reshape Indian education top to bottom - years later, is that reshaping actually visible on the ground, or mostly still sitting in the policy document?
points_for: Multidisciplinary degree structures, increased vocational integration and revised curriculum frameworks have genuinely rolled out at many universities since 2020.
The policy has shifted national conversation and institutional planning toward skills-integration and flexibility, a meaningful change in direction even where full execution lags.
Early movers among well-resourced universities and states demonstrate the reforms are operationally achievable, providing a working template other institutions can eventually follow.
Structural reforms of this scale in any large federal country typically take a decade or more to fully embed; judging NEP as a failure only a few years in may be premature.
points_against: Many of NEP's more ambitious structural goals, like the four-year undergraduate norm and credit-bank portability, face slow, inconsistent adoption across India's vast and varied higher-ed landscape.
NEP's ambitions for teacher training, infrastructure and digital access require sustained funding that hasn't uniformly followed the policy announcement.
As with the Labour Codes and UCC, education being a concurrent subject means implementation quality depends heavily on individual state capacity and political will, not just central policy.

Without robust, standardised monitoring of implementation outcomes across states, it's genuinely hard to tell how much of NEP's rollout is substantive change versus rebranded continuity of the old system.

Under-resourced government institutions, which serve the majority of India's students, are the ones most likely to struggle with NEP's ambitious structural demands, meaning the gap between policy and reality may be worst exactly where it matters most.

topics.title: Should India's coaching-centre culture be regulated more tightly?
topics.hook: India's competitive-exam coaching industry (the 'Kota model') remains a multi-billion-rupee sector built substantially around student stress and high-stakes pressure.
topics.why: A genuinely India-specific, high-stakes education-and-mental-health debate worth including for its direct relevance to this batch's own educational background.
topics.starter: The Kota model has built a multi-billion-rupee industry on exam pressure - so is the fix tighter regulation of the coaching centres, or fixing the seat scarcity that created the demand for them in the first place?
points_for: Documented student mental-health crises linked to coaching-centre pressure make a strong case for mandatory wellbeing safeguards, not just academic-outcome regulation.
Some states and the Ministry of Education have already introduced age-and-hour guidelines for coaching centres, showing regulators themselves see a genuine problem worth addressing.

Mandatory safeguards like counselling access, capped study hours and transparent success-rate disclosure could improve student welfare without necessarily banning or crippling the industry's core function.

Unregulated advertising of inflated success rates by coaching centres can mislead families into unrealistic expectations and financial strain, a consumer-protection gap regulation could directly address.
points_against: Coaching centres exist because they demonstrably improve outcomes on competitive exams that determine access to limited seats - regulating them away doesn't fix the underlying scarcity problem driving demand.
Many argue the real fix is expanding quality seats in top institutions and reducing exam-based bottlenecks, not just regulating the coaching industry that has grown around that scarcity.
Heavy-handed regulation risks pushing the industry further into unregulated, informal, or online-only formats that are even harder to monitor for student wellbeing than today's visible institutions.
Families who can't afford formal coaching already rely on cheaper informal alternatives; overregulating the formal sector could simply shift the same pressures into less accountable settings.

Existing age-and-hour guidelines remain a partial, contested first step rather than a settled resolution, suggesting the practical design of 'the right amount' of regulation is still genuinely unresolved.

topics.title: Should India's reservation/quota system be revisited for a modern economy?
topics.hook: A foundational, still-contested Indian policy debate, made newly relevant as AI-driven hiring shifts change what 'equal opportunity' in the job market even means.
topics.why: A classic, high-stakes GD topic that rewards careful, evidence-based, non-inflammatory argument - good practice for handling genuinely sensitive topics with composure.
topics.starter: Reservation was designed to correct decades of social disadvantage - the real question for a modern economy isn't whether that goal still matters, but whether the current mechanism is still the right tool to get there.
points_for: Some argue caste-based criteria should be supplemented or replaced by economic-criteria-based affirmative action to better target genuine present-day need.

As skills-first, project-based hiring grows, the debate increasingly includes whether reservation frameworks account for this shift in how employability is actually assessed, suggesting the existing structure may need updating to stay relevant.

Even those who support reservation broadly often debate whether current caps, creamy-layer rules and coverage categories reflect today's social reality accurately, indicating room for calibration rather than wholesale rejection.

Decades of policy application provide enough data to evaluate which specific mechanisms have worked well and which haven't, an evidence base a fresh review could draw on rather than treating the current structure as untouchable.
points_against: Historical and ongoing social disadvantage hasn't been fully corrected by decades of policy, and representation gaps persist across education and employment.

Diluting caste-based criteria in favour of purely economic criteria risks overlooking non-economic forms of discrimination, like social exclusion and access barriers, that income level alone doesn't capture.

Reservation has constitutional backing tied specifically to historically disadvantaged groups; replacing it with a purely economic standard changes the policy's fundamental rationale, not just its mechanics.
Frequent revisiting of a sensitive, hard-won policy compromise risks reopening political and social conflict without a clear consensus replacement ready to take its place.

Representation gaps in higher education and public employment for historically marginalised groups remain measurable even today, suggesting the underlying justification for reservation hasn't yet run its course.

topics.title: English-medium or mother-tongue: which actually serves India's students better?
topics.hook: NEP 2020 explicitly recommends mother-tongue instruction through at least Grade 5, even as English-medium schooling remains the aspirational default for many Indian families.
topics.why: A genuinely contested education-policy question with real economic-mobility stakes, directly connected to the NEP implementation debate above.
topics.starter: Research says kids learn foundational concepts faster in their mother tongue - so why do so many Indian families still choose English-medium schools even when it might mean their child struggles more at the start?
points_for: Strong educational research shows children grasp foundational concepts faster when taught in a language they already think in, before transitioning to a second language.
NEP 2020 explicitly recommends mother-tongue instruction through at least Grade 5, reflecting a policy consensus grounded in established pedagogical research, not just tradition.

Learning foundational concepts in a familiar language builds stronger critical-thinking and comprehension skills that transfer more effectively to a second language later, rather than forcing early rote memorisation in an unfamiliar one.
Mother-tongue instruction can improve early retention and reduce dropout rates among first-generation learners who otherwise struggle simply to follow instruction in an unfamiliar language.
points_against: English fluency remains a strong, well-documented economic-mobility signal in India's job market, and many families reasonably prioritise it despite the research on early-learning outcomes.
Delaying English exposure risks leaving students at a competitive disadvantage in a globally connected, English-dominant higher-education and corporate environment.

India's linguistic diversity makes 'mother tongue' itself a complicated, non-uniform policy target across regions, unlike more linguistically homogeneous countries where such research is often drawn from.

Aspirational demand for English-medium schooling is already a real, revealed preference among Indian families, even in lower-income households, suggesting families are weighing trade-offs the research-only framing may underweight.

Many strong models use mother-tongue foundational instruction with structured, early English-language teaching alongside it, showing the either/or framing itself may be somewhat of a false choice in the best implementations.

topics.title: Can India's private space sector become a genuine global commercial player?
topics.hook: Private space investment in India crossed $618 million by March 2026 - a nearly six-fold rise in a few years - with Skyroot Aerospace becoming India's first space-tech unicorn.
topics.why: A fast-emerging, genuinely exciting innovation-policy topic with real 2026 momentum, good for closing a GD session on an ambitious, forward-looking note.
topics.starter: India's private space sector has gone from a single startup to over 400 in a decade, with a homegrown unicorn now doing orbital launches - so are we watching the birth of a genuine global space power, or just an early-stage funding story that hasn't been tested yet?
points_for: India already offers proven cost-effective launch capability through ISRO's track record and has grown from 1 to over 400 space startups in a decade, with real private funding backing them.
Liberalised FDI rules, up to 100% in some segments, IN-SPACe's streamlined authorisation process, and dedicated venture/technology funds reflect a genuine government bet on private-sector-led growth.
Skyroot Aerospace achieving a historic private orbital launch and becoming India's first space-tech unicorn is concrete proof of execution, not just funding momentum.
India's cost advantage in engineering talent and manufacturing could let private players compete on price in satellite launch and components even without matching the biggest global players' scale.
points_against: Global competitors like SpaceX and China's state-backed programme operate at a scale and pace India's still-young private sector hasn't matched, particularly in reusable heavy-launch capability.
India's space economy currently holds only 2-3% of the global market but targets roughly a five-fold expansion by the early 2030s - an ambitious but not yet proven trajectory.
Capital-intensive, long-gestation space ventures are especially vulnerable to funding-cycle downturns, unlike software-first startups that can iterate and pivot faster on less capital.
Building genuinely global commercial launch and satellite businesses requires decades of reliability track record that even well-funded new entrants can't shortcut, regardless of current momentum.
Much of the current growth is measured in funding and startup counts rather than revenue or profitable commercial contracts, making it too early to call the sector a proven global commercial success.

latest.text: India's private space sector crossed $618.5 million in cumulative investment, with Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 achieving a historic private orbital launch and becoming India's first space-tech unicorn.

topics.title: How should India respond to rising US tariffs and trade protectionism?
topics.hook: Steep US tariff actions through 2025-26 have created real, measurable stress in India's export-oriented manufacturing sectors.
topics.why: A live geopolitical-economic question directly affecting the manufacturing, FMCG and consulting sectors covered elsewhere in this GD bank.
topics.starter: When a trading partner as important as the US imposes tariffs, does India protect its leverage by hitting back, or protect the relationship by sitting down to negotiate?
points_for: Matching tariffs signal that India won't simply absorb unilateral trade pressure, protecting domestic industry and maintaining negotiating leverage.
Tariff pressure has, in some sectors, accelerated India's own China+1 and PLI-driven manufacturing push, turning external pressure into a partial catalyst for domestic capability-building.
A firm stance signals to other trading partners that India won't be an easy target for future unilateral pressure, protecting its broader negotiating position beyond just this dispute.

Reliance on any single export market becomes a strategic vulnerability; a firmer response can be paired with actively diversifying export markets to reduce future exposure to any one country's trade policy.
points_against: Given the depth of India-US economic ties, a prolonged tariff standoff risks larger mutual damage than either side can easily absorb - negotiation often serves both economies better than escalation.

GST 2.0's rate rationalisation was explicitly framed by policymakers as helping offset external risks including steep US tariff actions, suggesting India's actual strategy leans toward absorbing and adapting rather than pure retaliation.
Export-oriented sectors already under tariff stress could face further, compounding damage if a retaliatory spiral escalates rather than resolves the underlying dispute.
India's relative economic and military leverage versus the US is asymmetric, making prolonged confrontation a riskier strategy for India than for a larger, more diversified US economy.
A negotiated settlement preserves the broader strategic partnership across defence, technology and investment ties that a purely trade-focused retaliatory approach could put at risk.

latest.text: GST 2.0's rate rationalisation was explicitly framed by policymakers as helping offset external risks including steep US tariff actions affecting Indian exports.

topics.title: Should India pursue a permanent UN Security Council seat more aggressively?
topics.hook: India's case for a permanent UNSC seat remains one of the most consistent asks in Indian foreign policy, even as Security Council reform has stalled for decades.
topics.why: A classic international-relations GD topic, good for testing structured argument on a genuinely difficult, slow-moving diplomatic question.
topics.starter: India's economy and global weight keep growing while its case for a permanent UNSC seat keeps stalling - so is it finally time to push harder, or has decades of patience taught us that pushing harder just isn't how this gets won?
points_for: India's population, economic scale and role in global institutions, from the G20 presidency to growing defence and space capability, make its continued exclusion from permanent UNSC membership increasingly anomalous.
A more assertive push raises the political cost of continued exclusion and keeps the issue visible on the global agenda rather than letting it quietly stall.
India's growing economic and strategic weight gives it more leverage today to press the case than it had decades ago when the reform debate first stalled.
Waiting indefinitely for consensus among existing permanent members, who have every incentive to preserve their own veto power, may mean the reform never happens unless pushed harder.
points_against: UNSC reform requires consensus among existing permanent members, several of whom have their own competing regional-power concerns - aggressive unilateral pushing without broader coalition-building may not accelerate the outcome.
India has long coordinated with Brazil, Germany and Japan as the G4 precisely because collective pressure has more diplomatic weight than pursuing the seat alone.
Even strong supporters acknowledge structural UNSC reform is unlikely in the near term given how difficult it is to get existing permanent members to dilute their own veto power.

Overly aggressive unilateral diplomacy risks straining bilateral relationships that India needs for other priorities like trade and defence cooperation, without materially improving the odds of reform.

India already exercises significant global influence through other channels, such as the G20 and the Quad, that don't depend on UNSC reform succeeding, reducing the urgency of an aggressive single-issue push.

topics.title: Is India's startup unicorn culture creating real value, or mostly recycling capital?
topics.hook: India now has 94+ unicorns and 600,000+ startups, but the 2022-24 funding correction exposed how much of that early valuation growth wasn't backed by durable unit economics.
topics.why: A useful, skeptical closing lens on the startup-ecosystem optimism already present across several sector-specific debates in this GD bank.
topics.starter: India now has more than 90 unicorns - but after the funding correction exposed how many of those valuations weren't backed by real unit economics, is that number actually a measure of value created, or just how much capital got recycled?
points_for: India's startup ecosystem has built real, lasting infrastructure - UPI-linked fintech, quick-commerce logistics, GCC-adjacent tech talent - that didn't exist a decade ago, unicorn status aside.
Investors now demanding proven unit economics before funding, rather than pure growth, can be read as the ecosystem maturing into a more durable, value-creating phase.

A healthy 2025-26 IPO pipeline in D2C and fintech will be a genuine, market-verified test of whether India's unicorn valuations reflect real, durable value - public markets are far harder to fool than late-stage private rounds.
India now has 94+ unicorns and 600,000+ startups, a base broad enough that even a meaningful minority of genuinely durable businesses represents substantial real value creation for the economy.
points_against: Some unicorn valuations reflected momentum-driven late-stage funding rounds more than durable business fundamentals, as the sharp 2022-24 correction later revealed.
The 2022-24 correction itself is direct evidence that a meaningful share of prior 'value creation' was valuation inflation rather than durable business performance.
Down-rounds and write-downs during the correction suggest some of the capital deployed simply moved between investors and founders without ever converting into lasting productive assets or jobs.

Heavy reliance on late-stage funding rounds to mark up valuations, rather than revenue or profit growth, made much of the 'unicorn' status more a function of fundraising skill than commercial success.

Investors demanding proven unit economics only now, after the correction, could just as easily be read as an admission that the earlier era overvalued growth without enough scrutiny in the first place.

latest.text: Inc42 frames 2026 as a 'rebalancing year' for Indian startups after a more disciplined 2025 - capital is flowing again, but concentrated in companies demonstrating real unit economics rather than growth alone.

topics.title: Should capital punishment be abolished in India?
topics.hook: A perennial ethics-and-law GD topic, worth including for its enduring relevance to justice-system and human-rights debate rounds.
topics.why: A classic, high-composure topic - useful for practicing balanced, evidence-based argument on an emotionally charged subject without losing structure.
topics.starter: For crimes we all agree are the worst imaginable, does execution deliver the justice we think it does - or does an irreversible punishment simply carry too much risk in a justice system that sometimes gets it wrong?
points_for: Proponents argue it serves as a proportionate response and deterrent for the 'rarest of rare' crimes, a standard India's courts already apply narrowly.
The Supreme Court's 'rarest of rare' doctrine already significantly restricts when capital punishment can be applied, meaning it functions as an exceptional remedy rather than a routine punishment.
For crimes causing extreme, irreversible harm, some victims' families and segments of the public view capital punishment as the only proportionate form of justice available.
Removing capital punishment entirely eliminates a sentencing option lawmakers and courts may consider genuinely necessary for the most extreme, universally condemned crimes.
points_against: Critics point to the irreversibility of execution against a justice system prone to wrongful convictions, and note limited empirical evidence that capital punishment deters crime better than life imprisonment.
A majority of countries have abolished capital punishment in law or practice, though India, the US and China remain notable exceptions that still actively use it.

India's justice system faces well-documented delays and inconsistencies in evidence and legal representation quality, especially for poorer defendants, raising the real risk that death sentences are applied unevenly.
Life imprisonment without parole can achieve the same incapacitation and public-safety goal as execution while preserving the ability to correct a wrongful conviction.

The debate is often more about frequency and cases than a binary keep/abolish choice, since India's 'rarest of rare' doctrine already limits application - a genuinely contested question remains whether even that narrow application is justified.

topics.title: Is India's education system still built for an industrial-era economy, not an AI-era one?
topics.hook: This is a fitting closer: it ties together the AI-and-jobs disruption, the skills-vs-degree debate, and the NEP-implementation question already raised elsewhere in this bank.
topics.why: A genuinely reflective, high-level topic to close a GD session on - synthesising several of this bank's live 2026 threads into one big-picture question.
topics.starter: We spend sixteen-plus years in an education system built to produce reliable, similarly-skilled graduates - so is that system actually preparing any of us for an economy where AI is redefining what 'skilled' even means?
points_for: Standardised, exam-heavy, degree-centric education was designed to produce large numbers of similarly-skilled workers for an economy of stable, well-defined jobs - a model AI-driven, specialised hiring is actively moving away from.
Freshers now make up just 13% of active tech job openings even as India's overall employability score has risen - a sign the skills produced and the skills demanded aren't yet well aligned.

Standardised testing rewards memorisation and speed under exam conditions, capabilities increasingly commoditised by AI tools themselves, rather than the judgment and adaptability an AI-era economy actually needs.
The pace of AI-driven change in job requirements is fast enough that curriculum-and-accreditation cycles, which typically take years to update, structurally lag behind what employers need right now.
points_against: NEP's multidisciplinary and skills-integration reforms, alongside the real growth of bootcamps and industry-aligned upskilling, suggest meaningful, if uneven, adaptation is already underway.

India's Skills Report 2026 shows employability rising to 56.3% even as project-based, skills-first hiring rose 38% YoY, indicating the system and the market are moving in the same direction, just not yet in sync.

Private-sector upskilling platforms, corporate training partnerships and campus-industry tie-ups are increasingly filling the gap faster than the formal curriculum cycle can, showing the broader ecosystem is adapting even where the core system lags.

Some foundational skills the industrial-era system still teaches well, like quantitative reasoning, structured writing and domain fundamentals, remain genuinely necessary inputs for succeeding in AI-era, skills-first hiring, not obsolete baggage to discard.

For students actively building interview-prep and skills infrastructure of their own, this question isn't abstract - it's the direct context shaping how they navigate the job market today, and dismissing the system entirely as 'industrial-era' risks underrating the genuine reform already in motion.

latest.text: India's Skills Report 2026 shows employability rising to 56.3% even as project-based, skills-first hiring rose 38% YoY - a real-time test of whether India's education system is adapting quickly enough.

topics.title: Should Starlink be allowed into India - and can satellite broadband really compete with Jio and Airtel's fibre?
topics.hook: Starlink has built 20 gateway sites in India and says Indian user data will stay in India, but as of October 2026 it still cannot switch on commercial service - it is waiting for spectrum and final security clearance.
topics.why: It packs telecom competition, digital inclusion, spectrum pricing and national security into one debate - and India's own telecom giants are on both sides of it, as competitors and as Starlink's distribution partners.
topics.starter: India already has some of the world's cheapest mobile data and fibre in most cities. So is Starlink the answer for the slice of India that fibre will never reach - or a premium product still looking for a market?
points_for: Satellite broadband reaches what fibre and towers can't do economically: hill states, islands, border villages, ships, aircraft and disaster zones. Low-earth-orbit satellites (roughly 550 km up) also give far lower latency than older geostationary satellite internet.
It works as a resilience layer - when floods, cyclones or cable cuts take down terrestrial networks, a satellite link keeps hospitals, banks and relief teams connected.

The incumbents themselves see room for it: in March 2025 both Jio and Airtel signed deals with SpaceX to sell and install Starlink equipment through their retail networks, treating it as complementary rather than purely a rival.
More players (Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb, Jio-SES) mean more competition and choice in a market where geostationary providers have had the space largely to themselves.

Enterprise demand is real even if consumer demand is uncertain - maritime, aviation, remote mining and energy sites, defence logistics and rural bank branches all need connectivity where fibre doesn't go.
points_against: Price: reports put indicative plans around ₹2,500-3,500 a month plus costly dish hardware, while urban fibre plans cost a fraction of that and offer higher, steadier speeds. In cities, satellite simply can't win on value.

Capacity is shared across each coverage cell, so speeds fall as more users join; early reports said the government expected initial caps of about 20 lakh users and up to 200 Mbps so satellite services don't undercut existing telecom networks.

Level playing field: mobile operators paid tens of thousands of crores for spectrum at auction, while satellite spectrum is being assigned administratively for a percentage of revenue - TRAI recommended 4% of adjusted gross revenue plus a per-user urban fee. Telcos argued this was unfair before the government sided with administrative allocation.

Sovereignty and security: a foreign-owned constellation carrying Indian traffic raises questions; a former Union Secretary argued satellite spectrum should be reserved for strategic and defence use, and DoT's security conditions now require network traffic and monitoring systems to sit inside India.

Dependence and sustainability: thousands of satellites from a single company raise concerns about space debris, astronomical interference and over-reliance on one private operator for critical connectivity.

latest.text: Starlink received its satcom (GMPCS) licence from the Department of Telecommunications after agreeing to India's national security conditions for satellite operators.
India's space regulator IN-SPACe granted Starlink a five-year authorisation - the last licence it needed before spectrum allocation.
The Digital Communications Commission signed off on most of TRAI's recommendations on how satellite spectrum should be priced and allocated; the framework now goes to the Cabinet for final approval.

Starlink said it has built 20 gateway sites and will keep Indian user data in India. Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications all hold permissions, but none can launch commercially without spectrum and second-stage security clearance.

topics.title: India's blanket ban on real-money online games - protecting citizens, or killing a legitimate industry?
topics.hook: Since 1 May 2026, the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act bans every online game played for money - whether skill or chance - along with its advertising and payments. The Supreme Court is now hearing challenges to it.
topics.why: It is a sharp test of how far the state should go to protect citizens from themselves, set against the right to do business, tax revenue, startup jobs and sports sponsorship.
topics.starter: Courts have long treated fantasy cricket and rummy as games of skill. So should a skill game played for money be treated like gambling - or did the government make the right call by drawing one simple, enforceable line?
points_for: The government's case rests on real harm: addiction, debt and financial ruin among young and low-income users, which a regulatory patchwork had failed to contain.
Authorities have linked unchecked growth of money gaming to fraud, money laundering and tax evasion; a clean prohibition is far easier to enforce than case-by-case 'skill vs chance' tests.
The Act doesn't ban gaming itself - it explicitly promotes e-sports and casual social games, steering the industry towards models that don't depend on users losing money.
Courts have recently backed state power in this area: in May 2026 the Supreme Court upheld Tamil Nadu's ban on online money games and the retrospective GST levied on them.
points_against: Petitioners argue a blanket ban is disproportionate and violates the constitutional right to carry on a lawful trade, because it treats genuine skill-based games the same as pure gambling.

Prohibition tends to push users offshore: one survey found the share of users spending more than two hours on offshore platforms jumped from 3.4% before the ban to 44% after it - beyond the reach of Indian consumer protection and taxes.
Regulation could have done the job: KYC, deposit limits, age-gating, self-exclusion and a licensing regulator are how many countries manage the same risks without wiping out an industry.
