The economic cost is large - jobs at gaming startups, government tax revenue (already hit by 28% GST on the full face value of bets) and sports sponsorship, which vanished from IPL 2026.

latest.text: Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act within days of its introduction; it received Presidential assent on 22 August 2025.
The Act and the Online Gaming Rules, 2026 came into force on 1 May, banning online money games, their advertising and related payments nationwide.
The Supreme Court agreed to a final hearing on the batch of petitions challenging the Act's constitutionality, alongside a PIL against gambling platforms posing as social or e-sports games.

topics.title: The US $100,000 H-1B fee - a setback for Indian talent, or a push to build more at home?
topics.hook: Since September 2025, US employers must pay $100,000 for each new H-1B petition - and in September 2026 Washington extended the fee for another year. Indians account for roughly 70% of H-1B holders.
topics.why: It directly affects the careers of Indian graduates, the business model of Indian IT services and the growth of Global Capability Centres in India - three things this batch's job market depends on.
topics.starter: If it now costs a US company $100,000 extra to bring an Indian engineer to America, is that a loss for India - or the best thing that could have happened to India's GCC story?
points_for: Work that can't move people to the US moves to India instead: analysts called the fee a push for companies to set up or expand GCCs here, creating senior, high-value roles at home.
It could slow brain drain - more experienced engineers and managers building careers and companies in India rather than abroad.
Indian IT firms had already cut their dependence on H-1Bs through local US hiring and offshore delivery, so the direct hit is smaller than the headline number suggests.
The fee applies only to new petitions, not to existing visa holders or renewals, limiting immediate disruption to people already working in the US.
points_against: It narrows one of the most valued career paths for Indian graduates and weakens the case for expensive US master's degrees that relied on H-1B access afterwards.
For many roles the fee matches or exceeds the employee's annual salary, so firms will simply stop sponsoring - one large Indian IT firm saw H-1B approvals fall 62% year on year in FY2026.
Onsite client work, pricing and margins for Indian IT services take a hit, at a time when revenue growth is already weak.
It signals a broader protectionist trend - including a proposed tax on outsourcing payments - that could hurt services exports beyond visas.

latest.text: A US presidential proclamation imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions filed from 21 September 2025, up from roughly $2,000-5,000 earlier.

The White House extended the fee for another year despite legal challenges; the Department of Homeland Security began rulemaking to raise it to about $103,000 and added checks on employers' layoffs of US workers.

topics.title: The India-EU free trade deal - a big win for Indian exporters, or a risk for Indian industry?
topics.hook: After nearly two decades of talks, India and the EU concluded a free trade agreement in January 2026 covering about a quarter of global GDP. Tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports to India will be removed or reduced.
topics.why: With US tariffs squeezing Indian exports, the EU deal is India's biggest bet on diversifying trade - and it touches manufacturing, jobs, consumer prices and climate rules at once.
topics.starter: India walked away from trade deals for years to protect domestic industry. Has the mood changed because the world has - and is the EU deal the right place to start opening up?
points_for: Diversification: labour-intensive exports like textiles, leather and jewellery, hit hard by steep US tariffs, gain preferential access to one of the world's richest markets.
Cheaper European machinery, chemicals, medical and optical equipment lower input costs for Indian manufacturers and hospitals.
It deepens a strategic partnership beyond trade, including defence and security cooperation, at a time when India wants more balanced global alliances.
Sensitive issues were left out to get the deal done, so the most politically fragile sectors are largely protected.
points_against: European cars, wines and processed foods will compete harder with Indian producers as tariffs fall, putting pressure on domestic firms that grew up behind high duties.
The EU's carbon border tax on steel, aluminium and other carbon-heavy imports could cancel out much of the tariff advantage for Indian exporters.
Concerns remain about intellectual-property terms affecting India's generic medicine industry and about EU standards acting as non-tariff barriers.
Ratification risk is real - the EU-Mercosur deal stalled for years after political conclusion, so gains may arrive later than promised.

latest.text: India and the EU announced the conclusion of FTA negotiations at their summit in New Delhi on 27 January 2026.
The EU's ambassador to India said both sides aim to sign the agreement by end-2026 and bring it into force in early 2027, once legal vetting and translation are complete.
Reports said the agreement is set to be signed on 16 December 2026, while a separate interim trade deal with the US remains pending.

topics.title: Should India ban social media for children under 16, like Australia?
topics.hook: Australia became the first country to ban under-16s from most social media in December 2025. India's Economic Survey has since suggested age-based limits, and the IT ministry has confirmed discussions are under way.
topics.why: It asks whether the state or parents should decide children's digital lives - and whether such a rule can work in a country with a billion internet users and widely shared phones.
topics.starter: We don't let 14-year-olds drive or drink. Is social media really different - or would a ban in India just push children onto fake accounts and VPNs while their parents look away?
points_for: Evidence on anxiety, sleep loss, cyberbullying and addictive design is growing, and children can't fairly be expected to resist products engineered to keep them scrolling.
A clear legal age shifts responsibility onto platforms to verify age, instead of leaving every parent to fight the battle alone.
Deepfakes, sextortion and harmful content targeting minors have made the risks more severe than when these platforms launched.
India wouldn't be alone: Australia, France and Malaysia have moved on age limits, and the DPDP Act already requires verifiable parental consent for processing children's data.
points_against: Age verification at India's scale is hard and risks creating new privacy problems if it relies on ID documents or Aadhaar-linked checks for every user.
Bans are easy to evade with borrowed phones, fake birthdays and VPNs, and could push children to less moderated corners of the internet.
Many young people learn, create and find community online - especially in small towns - and a blanket ban cuts off the good with the bad.
Digital literacy, default safety settings for minors, time limits and meaningful parental controls may achieve more than prohibition.

latest.text: India's Economic Survey recommended that the government consider age-based limits on social media use; a ruling-coalition MP drafted a private member's bill to bar under-16s from holding accounts.
The IT minister said discussions on regulating social media use by under-16s are under way, with partial, phased restrictions reported to be under consideration rather than a complete ban.

topics.title: 70-hour work weeks - the path to a developed India, or a recipe for burnout?
topics.hook: Prominent business leaders have urged young Indians to work 70 or even 90 hours a week to build the nation, setting off a fierce debate about productivity, wellbeing and who actually benefits from longer hours.
topics.why: Every fresher will face this question in their first job: is long-hours culture the price of growth, or a sign of poor management? It also ties into India's Labour Codes and the global four-day-week debate.
topics.starter: Countries like Japan and South Korea built their economies on brutal hours - and now struggle with burnout and falling birth rates. Should India copy the first half of that story, or learn from the second?
points_for: Catch-up growth has historically demanded intense effort; India is trying to compress decades of development into a generation.
Early-career years are when learning compounds fastest - extra hours in the first few years can build skills and networks that pay off for decades.
Founders and teams in competitive sectors often do work long hours, and some argue that ambition shouldn't be legislated away.
Productivity gaps are real; supporters see more hours as one lever while automation and skills catch up.
points_against: Research consistently shows output per hour drops sharply beyond roughly 50 hours a week; long hours often mean more presence, not more productivity.
ILO data already ranks India among the countries with the longest average working weeks, yet its productivity per hour remains low - the problem isn't effort.
Health, mental health and family costs are significant, and they fall hardest on women, who also carry most unpaid care work.
India's Labour Codes keep a 48-hour weekly limit for a reason; normalising 70-90 hours puts pressure on employees who can't afford to say no.

topics.title: Should freshers start their careers at a startup or a well-established firm?
topics.hook: A startup offers responsibility on day one; an established firm offers structure, training and a brand on your CV. For many final-placement students, this is the real choice behind every offer.
topics.why: It is personal and practical, so panels use it to see whether candidates can argue with nuance about their own careers instead of repeating clichés.
topics.starter: At a startup you might own a whole product line in year one. At a large firm you might own one slide of a deck. But which of those actually makes you better at your job five years from now?
points_for: Startup case: wider scope early - you touch product, sales, operations and customers, which builds judgement faster than a narrow role.
Startup case: closer access to founders and decision-makers, faster feedback and visible impact.
Startup case: ESOPs and fast promotions can create outsized upside if the company succeeds.
Startup case: the habit of working with limited resources and ambiguity is valuable everywhere later.
points_against: Established-firm case: structured training, mentorship and processes teach how good work is done at scale - foundations many startups never have time to teach.
Established-firm case: job security matters; many startups fold or cut staff within a few years, and funding cycles are unpredictable.
Established-firm case: a strong brand on the CV opens doors for later moves, higher studies and switching sectors.
Established-firm case: higher and steadier pay helps with education loans - and you can still join a startup later with better skills and a network.

topics.title: Is an MBA still worth it in the age of AI?
topics.hook: AI tools now draft analyses, decks and market reports in minutes - the kind of work many entry-level management roles were built around. So what exactly is an MBA graduate being paid for?
topics.why: A self-reflective topic that tests whether candidates understand where human value lies as AI changes white-collar work - and how they plan to stay relevant.
topics.starter: If an AI can build a competent financial model in 30 seconds, is the MBA's value now in what we know - or in how we think, decide and lead people?
points_for: AI raises the value of judgement, leadership, negotiation and stakeholder management - skills an MBA trains through cases, projects and teamwork.
Someone has to decide which problems to solve and take accountability for decisions; AI produces options, managers choose and own them.
The network, recruiter access and career switch an MBA enables don't depend on technical tasks that AI can automate.
Graduates who combine business understanding with AI fluency are likely to be more valuable, not less.
points_against: Many entry-level analyst tasks MBA hires were trained for - research, slide-making, basic modelling - are exactly what AI automates first.
Programmes that teach frameworks by rote risk producing generalists whose skills a tool can replicate cheaply.
Costs keep rising while starting salaries in some roles stagnate, weakening the return on investment.
Employers increasingly hire for demonstrated skills and portfolios over degrees, so the credential alone counts for less.

topics.title: Red vs Blue
topics.hook: A classic abstract GD topic. There is no right answer - the panel is watching how you interpret the two colours and build a structured argument around them.
topics.why: Abstract topics test creativity, structure and the ability to take a group somewhere interesting. Strong candidates propose a lens (business, psychology, politics, nature) and invite others to build on it.
topics.starter: Red is the colour of passion, danger and urgency; blue is calm, trust and depth. Maybe the real question is: does the world need more fire or more water right now?
points_for: Red: energy, ambition and urgency - the colour of action. Startups, sales and change need red thinking.
Red signals attention and alarm - in a noisy world, standing out matters; it's why so many brands and 'Sale' signs use it.
Red Ocean strategy: competing head-on in existing markets is where most businesses actually live, and winning there takes discipline.
Red as courage and sacrifice - the colour of revolutions and of blood donation alike.
points_against: Blue: calm, trust and stability - the colour of banks, hospitals and tech platforms that want users to feel safe.
Blue Ocean strategy: instead of fighting rivals, create uncontested markets - a smarter route than a red-ocean price war.
Blue as depth and reflection - the sky and the sea remind us to think long-term before acting.
A synthesis angle: red and blue together make purple - perhaps the best leaders and organisations combine urgency with calm.

topics.title: Zero
topics.hook: Zero can mean nothing - or the most powerful idea in mathematics. An abstract topic that rewards candidates who can move between meanings.
topics.why: It lets you show breadth: history (India's gift of zero to the world), business (zero-based budgeting, zero defects, zero waste), and life (starting from zero).
topics.starter: India gave the world zero, and with it modern mathematics, computing and finance. Funny that the idea of 'nothing' turned out to be worth everything.
points_for: Zero as origin: Indian mathematicians formalised zero as a number, without which place-value arithmetic, computers and modern finance wouldn't exist.
Zero as ambition: zero defects, zero accidents, net-zero emissions, zero hunger - targets that force breakthrough thinking rather than incremental change.
Zero as a fresh start: zero-based budgeting asks every rupee to justify itself, and starting from zero frees people and companies from legacy assumptions.
Zero as a multiplier: any number multiplied by zero is zero - one missing value like integrity or safety can wipe out everything else.
points_against: Zero as emptiness: zero balance, zero growth, zero opportunity - for millions of people, 'starting from zero' is not inspiring but a trap.
Zero-sum thinking: the belief that one person's gain must be another's loss poisons negotiations, politics and teamwork.
Zero tolerance policies can be blunt - rigid rules that ignore context sometimes cause more harm than the problem.
Chasing zero (risk, error, failure) can paralyse innovation; some failure is the price of learning.

topics.title: Is the world black and white, or shades of grey?
topics.hook: A topic about certainty versus nuance. It can be taken towards ethics, decision-making, leadership, law or even data and AI.
topics.why: Panels use it to see whether candidates can hold two ideas at once, and whether they recognise when clear rules work better than case-by-case judgement.
topics.starter: Our laws are written in black and white, but our judges spend their careers in the grey. Maybe the question isn't which one the world is - it's when we should act as if it's one or the other.
points_for: Some lines should be black and white: corruption, discrimination, safety violations and fraud need clear rules, not negotiation.
Clear rules create trust and predictability - people and businesses can plan when they know exactly where the line is.
Leaders often need to make decisive calls; endless nuance can become an excuse for inaction.
Binary choices sit at the heart of technology itself: every digital system is built on ones and zeros.
points_against: Most real decisions - business strategy, policy, relationships - involve trade-offs where context changes the right answer.
Black-and-white thinking drives polarisation; social media algorithms reward extreme positions and punish nuance.
Good managers judge situations, not just rules; the same mistake can mean carelessness in one case and courage in another.
Even data isn't black and white - AI models give probabilities, not certainties, and interpreting them responsibly requires judgement.

topics.title: Mirror
topics.hook: A mirror shows you what is in front of it - nothing more, nothing less. An abstract topic about self-reflection, honesty, perception and society.
topics.why: It rewards candidates who can connect a simple object to leadership, feedback culture, media and technology in an organised way.
topics.starter: A mirror never lies - but it also only shows what you choose to stand in front of it. Maybe that's the real lesson about self-reflection.
points_for: Self-reflection: honest self-assessment is the starting point of growth for people and organisations; great leaders seek feedback that shows them as they are.
Society's mirror: literature, cinema and journalism reflect a society's realities back to it, often forcing change.
Mirroring in communication: people trust those who listen and reflect their concerns, a core skill in sales, negotiation and leadership.
Accountability: transparent reporting, audits and data act as an organisation's mirror, showing what is really happening.
points_against: Mirrors only show the surface - appearance, not character - and a culture obsessed with image risks valuing looks over substance.
Social media works like a distorted mirror, showing curated versions of others' lives and warping how we see ourselves.
Algorithms mirror our existing views back at us, creating echo chambers instead of growth.
Reflection without action is just vanity; looking in the mirror is useless unless you change what you see.

topics.title: Silence
topics.hook: An abstract topic that is also a test in itself: in a GD where everyone is fighting to speak, what is the value of silence?
topics.why: Candidates who handle this well show self-awareness about the GD format, listening skills and the ability to argue for restraint without disappearing from the discussion.
topics.starter: In a room full of people trying to be heard, maybe the most powerful thing is the pause before you speak. Silence isn't absence - it can be strategy.
points_for: Listening is underrated: good leaders, negotiators and doctors speak less and understand more.
Strategic silence in negotiations makes the other side reveal more; a pause often carries more weight than a rushed reply.
Silence creates space for thinking and creativity in an age of constant notifications and noise.
Not every issue needs an opinion from everyone; restraint can be a sign of wisdom rather than weakness.
points_against: Silence in the face of wrongdoing is complicity - whistleblowers, journalists and citizens who speak up protect institutions.
In organisations, silence often hides problems; psychological safety exists precisely so people speak up early.
Silent majorities lose to loud minorities in politics and on social media; staying quiet cedes the narrative.
In a GD or interview, silence is read as lack of ideas - knowing when to break it matters as much as knowing when to keep it.

topics.title: A blank sheet of paper
topics.hook: An empty A4 sheet can represent possibility, fear, freedom or waste. A classic abstract prompt to see how candidates create a direction from nothing.
topics.why: It tests creativity and structure together - the best participants pick a lens (careers, innovation, policy, environment) and give the group a framework to build on.
topics.starter: Every startup, policy and masterpiece began as a blank sheet of paper. The question is whether we see it as freedom - or as the fear of getting the first line wrong.
points_for: Possibility: a blank sheet has no constraints - the 'first principles' mindset that lets innovators rethink a problem instead of copying past answers.
Fresh starts: new graduates, new governments and new companies get a rare chance to design without legacy baggage.
Equality: everyone gets the same blank page; what differs is how they fill it, which makes effort and imagination the real differentiators.
Simplicity: sometimes the best design, essay or strategy keeps a lot of the page empty - clarity comes from what you leave out.
points_against: Blank-page paralysis is real: too much freedom can freeze people; constraints often drive creativity.
Nobody truly starts blank - background, privilege and access to resources shape what each person can write.
Starting from scratch can be wasteful; building on what already works is often smarter than reinventing it.
An environmental angle: a sheet of paper costs trees, water and energy - a reminder that even 'nothing' has a cost.

topics.title: Freebies vs welfare - smart social spending, or fiscal irresponsibility?
topics.hook: From free electricity and bus rides to monthly cash transfers for women, poll promises keep growing. Supporters call it welfare; critics call it 'revdi culture' that states can't afford.
topics.why: It goes to the heart of public finance, electoral politics and what a developing country owes its poorest citizens - and the line between welfare and freebie is genuinely contested.
topics.starter: One person's freebie is another person's safety net. So the real question isn't whether states should spend on citizens - it's which spending builds a future and which just buys the next election.
points_for: Direct cash transfers to women have been linked to better household nutrition, school attendance and women's financial independence - this is welfare, not waste.
Free or subsidised essentials like school meals, healthcare and basic electricity have long-term payoffs in productivity and human capital.
Corporate tax breaks and loan write-offs are rarely called 'freebies', yet they also cost the exchequer - the label is often applied selectively to spending on the poor.
In an economy with weak social security and huge informal employment, transfers cushion households against shocks that markets don't.
points_against: When states borrow to fund recurring giveaways, interest costs crowd out spending on roads, schools and hospitals that would create lasting value.
Unconditional freebies announced just before elections look more like vote-buying than policy, and are hard to withdraw once started.
Free electricity and water can encourage overuse - for example, groundwater depletion from free farm power - and weaken utilities' finances.
Better-targeted schemes, sunset clauses and honest budgeting of their cost would protect welfare while keeping state finances sustainable.

topics.title: Should India host the 2036 Olympics?
topics.hook: India is officially in the race: in October 2026 the IOC confirmed it among seven bidders for 2036, with Ahmedabad at the centre of the bid. The host is due to be chosen in 2029.
topics.why: A classic cost-benefit debate - national pride, soft power and sports culture versus huge spending, debt risk and opportunity cost in a country with pressing basic needs.
topics.starter: India has won fewer Olympic medals in its entire history than some countries win at a single Games. Should we host the Olympics to build a sporting culture - or build the sporting culture first?
points_for: Hosting accelerates infrastructure - transport, housing, urban renewal - that cities need anyway, and compresses decades of planning into a deadline.
It is a soft-power statement on a global stage, boosting tourism, investment and India's image as a confident, capable nation.
A home Games can transform grassroots sport, as funding, facilities and attention flow into athletics, swimming and other non-cricket sports.
Ahmedabad is already hosting the 2030 Commonwealth Games, giving India a practical rehearsal and reusable venues.
points_against: Many recent hosts saw costs balloon far beyond budgets, leaving debt and 'white elephant' stadiums that sit empty afterwards.
The same money could fund thousands of schools, sports academies and coaching programmes that build athletes more directly.
India's 2010 Commonwealth Games are still remembered for delays and corruption allegations - execution risk is real.
Medal success comes from long-term systems - talent identification, coaching and sports science - not from hosting a single event.

latest.text: India formally submitted Ahmedabad's bid for the 2030 Commonwealth Games, seen as a stepping stone towards the 2036 Olympic bid.
The IOC confirmed India and Qatar among seven bidders for 2036; a shortlist is due in March and the host will be chosen by a contested vote in 2029.

topics.title: Can India become a global semiconductor hub?
topics.hook: India started commercial chip production in 2026 - a memory-chip assembly and testing plant in Gujarat was the first to go live - and the government has approved a second phase of the Semiconductor Mission.
topics.why: Chips sit at the centre of AI, electric vehicles, defence and smartphones. Whether India can build a real chip industry is a test of its manufacturing ambitions and its strategic independence.
topics.starter: Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced chips. India now makes some chips too. Is that the start of a genuine industry - or are we subsidising factories that will never be globally competitive?
points_for: The first wave has arrived on schedule: assembly, testing and packaging plants began commercial production in 2026, and 12 projects were approved under the first phase of the mission.
Supply-chain diversification away from East Asia gives India a real opening, as global companies look for 'China+1' and Taiwan-risk hedges.
India already has a deep chip-design talent pool - a large share of the world's chip designers work here - giving it an edge in the most valuable part of the value chain.
A domestic chip base reduces strategic dependence for defence, telecom and critical infrastructure.
points_against: Most early projects are assembly and packaging, not cutting-edge fabrication, which captures far less value and know-how.
Leading-edge fabs need huge, steady supplies of ultra-pure water, stable power and specialised chemicals - areas where India's ecosystem is still thin.
Heavy subsidies - often half the capital cost - are expensive, and global rivals like the US and EU are offering similar incentives.
It takes decades to build the expertise Taiwan and South Korea have; India risks spreading money across too many projects instead of a few winners.

latest.text: India's first commercial semiconductor production began with the inauguration of a memory-chip assembly and testing plant in Sanand, Gujarat.

Three ISM 1.0 projects had started commercial production, with officials expecting five to six by end-2026; the Cabinet approved ISM 2.0 covering design, fabs, packaging, equipment, materials and R&D.

topics.title: Should the RBI defend the rupee, or let it weaken to help exports?
topics.hook: The rupee has fallen more than 7% against the dollar in 2026 and is hovering near its record low of about 97, despite heavy RBI intervention that has drawn down India's forex reserves.
topics.why: Currency policy affects inflation, fuel prices, foreign education costs, exporters' competitiveness and foreign investor confidence - all at once, and with real trade-offs.
topics.starter: A weaker rupee makes our software and textiles cheaper abroad but our oil and iPhones more expensive at home. So who should the RBI be protecting - exporters or consumers?
points_for: Defend: India imports most of its crude oil, so a falling rupee feeds directly into fuel prices and inflation that hurt the poor most.
Defend: sharp, disorderly falls can trigger panic and capital flight; the RBI's job is to smooth volatility and keep confidence.
Defend: companies and students with dollar liabilities - foreign loans, overseas tuition - face rising costs when the rupee slides.
Defend: a stable currency supports India's goal of internationalising the rupee for trade settlement.
points_against: Let it adjust: burning reserves to fight market forces is costly and can't last; the RBI has also had to use higher interest rates, which slow growth.
Let it adjust: a weaker rupee makes Indian exports more competitive at a time when US tariffs are squeezing exporters.
Let it adjust: the rupee's fall reflects global factors - a strong dollar, high oil prices, foreign investors pulling out about $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026 - that intervention can't fix.
Let it adjust: a flexible exchange rate acts as a shock absorber; defending a level often just delays the adjustment.

latest.text: The rupee hit a record low of about 96.97 per dollar amid high oil prices and foreign outflows.
The rupee was again within 0.2% of its record low, down more than 7% in 2026, with reports noting the RBI's intervention has sharply reduced forex reserves.

topics.title: AI regulation - should India follow the EU's strict rulebook, or stay light-touch?
topics.hook: The EU has a binding, risk-based AI Act. India has chosen voluntary AI governance guidelines that lean on existing laws - but in 2026 it also notified its first binding rules on AI-generated content.
topics.why: AI will shape every job this batch is entering. How a country regulates it decides how fast startups can build, how safe citizens are, and who is accountable when AI causes harm.
topics.starter: Regulate too early and you kill an industry before it's born; regulate too late and you're cleaning up harms you could have prevented. Where should India draw the line?
points_for: Strict rules (EU-style): high-risk uses like hiring, lending, policing and healthcare need clear obligations, audits and accountability before harm is done.
Strict rules: deepfakes, fraud and biased algorithms already affect millions; voluntary guidelines rarely change company behaviour.
Strict rules: Indian firms serving Europe must comply with the EU AI Act anyway, so aligning standards reduces confusion.
Strict rules: clear law gives citizens rights to explanation and redress, building the trust AI adoption needs.
points_against: Light-touch: India is still building its AI industry; heavy compliance costs favour big global firms over Indian startups.
Light-touch: existing laws - the IT Act, DPDP Act, criminal and consumer law - already cover most concrete harms like fraud, defamation and non-consensual imagery.
Light-touch: technology moves faster than legislation; flexible sector-specific guidance from regulators like RBI and SEBI can adapt quicker.
Light-touch: targeted binding rules for specific harms, like labelling AI-generated content, can address risks without a single omnibus law.

latest.text: MeitY released the India AI Governance Guidelines, a voluntary, light-touch framework that relies on existing laws and sectoral regulators rather than a standalone AI Act.
MeitY notified IT Intermediary Amendment Rules, 2026 - India's first binding rules on AI-generated content - effective 20 February 2026.

topics.title: Delhi's air pollution - should it be treated as a national health emergency?
topics.hook: Every winter, Delhi-NCR's air quality slips into 'severe', schools halt outdoor activities and emergency GRAP curbs kick in - as they did again in January 2026, when the AQI crossed 400.
topics.why: It is a recurring public health crisis that tests governance across states, sectors and seasons - and a classic GD on whether emergency responses can fix a structural problem.
topics.starter: We declare emergencies for floods that last a week. Delhi breathes hazardous air for months every year. Why is that not treated as an emergency?
points_for: The health toll is enormous - polluted air is linked to heart disease, lung disease and shorter life expectancy, with children and the elderly hit hardest.
Emergency status would give a single authority powers and funding across Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and UP, ending the blame game between states.
Seasonal measures under GRAP only react once air is already toxic; an emergency framing would force year-round action on root causes.
The economic cost - sick days, lower productivity, tourism and talent avoiding the city - is large enough to justify extraordinary measures.
points_against: Pollution comes from many sources - vehicles, construction dust, industry, crop burning, weather - and needs long-term structural fixes, not emergency theatre.
Emergency powers can be blunt and unfair, hurting daily-wage workers, small businesses and farmers through sudden bans.
The tools already exist - the Commission for Air Quality Management, GRAP and clean-air programmes - the problem is enforcement, not legal status.
Focusing only on Delhi ignores that many other Indian cities have similarly poor air with far less attention.

latest.text: Delhi's average AQI crossed 400 into the 'severe' category, and the Commission for Air Quality Management invoked Stage IV of the Graded Response Action Plan.

topics.title: Caste census - better policymaking, or deeper social divisions?
topics.hook: Census 2027 will count caste for all communities - the first full caste enumeration since 1931. House-listing ran from April to September 2026; people will be counted in February 2027.
topics.why: Reservations, welfare targeting and political representation all depend on caste data that India hasn't collected in nearly a century - making this one of the most consequential policy debates of the decade.
topics.starter: We make caste-based policy every day using data from 1931. Is counting caste the way to finally make that policy fair - or will it make caste even more central to Indian life?
points_for: Policy needs data: reservations and welfare schemes are designed without reliable current numbers, which a census can provide with legal backing.
Accurate data can show which communities have actually benefited and which remain left behind, enabling better targeting.
You can't fix an inequality you refuse to measure; caste already shapes access to education, jobs and land.
Unlike the 2011 socio-economic caste survey, whose caste data was never released, the census carries the statutory backing of the Census Act.
points_against: Counting caste may harden identities and fuel competitive politics over quotas, rather than moving society beyond caste.
Data quality is a serious risk - the 2011 survey recorded over 46 lakh distinct caste names, many duplicates and misspellings, making the data unusable.
Results could trigger demands to breach the 50% reservation ceiling and reopen settled political questions.
Economic criteria like income and assets might target welfare more precisely than caste alone.

latest.text: The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs decided to include caste enumeration in the next Census.
The first phase of Census 2027 - house-listing - began on 1 April, running to 30 September 2026; caste will be recorded during population enumeration in February 2027.

topics.title: Is brain drain actually bad for India?
topics.hook: Millions of Indian graduates have moved abroad for study and work. Some call it a loss of the country's best talent; others call it a global network that sends money, ideas and investment home.
topics.why: It is directly relevant to this batch's own choices, and it forces candidates to weigh national, economic and personal perspectives.
topics.starter: When an Indian engineer leads a global tech company, do we count that as India's loss - or India's win?
points_for: It is a loss: India subsidises elite education, then other economies capture the returns when graduates leave.
It is a loss: shortages of doctors, researchers and top engineers at home slow innovation and public services.
It is a loss: when the most ambitious leave, fewer people are left to build institutions and start companies in India.
It is a loss: it signals problems - research funding, bureaucracy, quality of life - that need fixing.
points_against: It is a gain: India is the world's largest recipient of remittances, a major source of foreign exchange.
It is a gain: the diaspora brings back investment, global networks and expertise - many Indian startups and GCCs were seeded by returnees.
It is 'brain circulation', not drain: people increasingly return, especially as opportunities in India grow.
It is a gain: Indians in senior global roles boost India's soft power and influence policy in India's favour.

topics.title: Should voting be compulsory in India?
topics.hook: Around a third of eligible voters typically don't vote in Indian general elections. Countries like Australia and Belgium make voting compulsory - should India?
topics.why: A democracy-and-rights debate that tests whether candidates can balance civic duty, individual freedom and practical enforcement.
topics.starter: If voting is a right, can the state force you to use it? And if it's a duty, why do we let a third of the country skip it?
points_for: Higher turnout makes governments more representative of all citizens, not just the most motivated or mobilised groups.
It would push parties to appeal to the whole electorate rather than focusing only on core vote banks.
Urban middle-class turnout is often low; compulsory voting would bring their concerns into politics.
A 'None of the Above' option already exists, so compulsion still allows people to register dissent.
points_against: Forcing people to vote infringes personal liberty; the freedom not to vote is part of democratic choice.
Enforcement in a country of nearly a billion voters - many migrant workers away from home - would be impractical and could penalise the poor.
Uninterested voters forced to the booth may vote randomly, adding noise rather than meaning.
Better solutions exist: remote voting for migrants, easier registration and civic education raise turnout without coercion.

topics.title: Job-hopping vs loyalty - is staying long at one company outdated?
topics.hook: Many young professionals switch jobs every 18-24 months for raises and new skills, while employers complain about 'loyalty-less' hiring. Which approach builds a better career?
topics.why: Every fresher will face this choice; the panel wants to see whether you understand career capital, not just salary.
topics.starter: Switching jobs is often the fastest way to a raise. But is it also the fastest way to never becoming truly good at anything?
points_for: For job-hopping: external moves typically bring bigger salary jumps than internal increments.
For job-hopping: exposure to different companies, managers and industries builds broad skills and networks quickly.
For job-hopping: companies rarely show loyalty in layoffs, so expecting one-sided loyalty from employees is unfair.
For job-hopping: early-career exploration helps people find the role that actually fits them.
points_against: For loyalty: deep expertise and trust take years; people who stay often get bigger responsibilities and leadership roles.
For loyalty: frequent switches can look like a red flag to recruiters for senior roles.
For loyalty: you rarely see the full impact of your work - a product launch, a turnaround - if you leave every year.
For loyalty: internal moves can offer variety without losing relationships and reputation.

topics.title: Moonlighting and side hustles - should employers allow them?
topics.hook: From freelance design to content creation and trading, many professionals now earn outside their day job. Some companies call it a conflict of interest; others encourage it.
topics.why: It touches employment law, ethics, productivity and the creator economy - and it's increasingly a question candidates get asked directly.
topics.starter: If a company doesn't own your weekends, why should it control what you do with them?
points_for: What employees do in their own time is their business, as long as there's no conflict of interest or misuse of company resources.
Side projects build skills, creativity and entrepreneurship that often benefit the main job.
Extra income offers financial security in an era of layoffs and stagnant salaries.
Banning it pushes it underground; clear policies are more realistic and build trust.
points_against: Working for a competitor or client creates genuine conflicts of interest and risks to confidential information.
Second jobs can cause fatigue and divided attention, hurting performance in the primary role.
Full-time pay assumes full-time commitment, and teams depend on people being available.
Some contracts and regulated sectors legally restrict outside work, making blanket permission risky.

topics.title: Employee monitoring software - productivity tool or workplace surveillance?
topics.hook: With remote and hybrid work, more companies track keystrokes, screenshots, app usage and even webcam activity. Is this good management or a breach of trust?
topics.why: It combines privacy law (including India's DPDP Act), HR strategy and ethics - a strong test of balanced reasoning.
topics.starter: If you need software to know whether your team is working, is the problem the employees - or the management?
points_for: Companies have a legitimate interest in protecting data, preventing fraud and meeting security and compliance requirements.
Activity data can reveal workload imbalances, burnout risks and process bottlenecks.
In remote setups, some visibility helps fair evaluation and accountability.
Transparent monitoring with clear policies is better than suspicion and micromanagement.
points_against: Tracking keystrokes and screenshots measures activity, not outcomes, and rewards looking busy over real work.
Constant surveillance damages trust, morale and creativity, and can push good people to leave.
It raises serious privacy concerns, especially on personal devices; data protection law requires purpose limitation and consent.
Managing by goals and results is a more effective way to ensure productivity.

topics.title: Should listed companies have mandatory quotas for women in leadership?
topics.hook: Indian law already requires at least one woman director on many company boards, yet women remain rare in CEO and senior management roles. Should quotas go further?
topics.why: Diversity, meritocracy and corporate governance collide here - and panels watch how candidates handle a sensitive topic with evidence and balance.
topics.starter: Mandating one woman director got women into boardrooms. Did it change who actually runs companies - and would a bigger quota?
points_for: Without mandates, progress is painfully slow; structural barriers don't disappear by themselves.
Research links diverse leadership teams to better decision-making and governance.
Visible women leaders change the pipeline, encouraging more women to stay and aim for senior roles.
Countries such as Norway used board quotas to rapidly change representation.
points_against: Quotas can lead to tokenism - appointing women to tick boxes, sometimes from the same small circle or promoters' families.
They can undermine the perceived merit of women who earn their positions.
The real bottleneck is the pipeline - women leaving mid-career due to caregiving and workplace culture - which quotas at the top don't fix.
Better parental leave, flexible work, childcare and mentorship may deliver deeper change than mandates.

topics.title: Gen Z at work - a different work ethic, or just different expectations?
topics.hook: Managers often say Gen Z won't stay late, quits quickly and demands flexibility. Gen Z says they simply refuse to accept burnout and want purpose. Who's right?
topics.why: This batch is Gen Z. The panel wants to see whether you can discuss your own generation honestly, without being defensive or stereotyping.
topics.starter: Every generation called the next one lazy. Is Gen Z really different - or are workplaces finally being asked questions they should have answered long ago?
points_for: Gen Z's expectations are healthy: setting boundaries, wanting mental-health support and refusing toxic cultures improves workplaces for everyone.
They are digital natives, quick to adopt tools and AI, bringing real productivity gains.
Wanting purpose, feedback and growth is a reasonable demand, not entitlement.
Job-hopping reflects a job market where companies offer little security, not a lack of commitment.
points_against: Some managers see lower tolerance for routine, grinding work that every career requires at the start.
Constant job changes can mean shallower skills and fewer people willing to stay through tough phases.
Over-reliance on remote and asynchronous work can weaken mentorship and learning that happen in person.
Generalising about any generation is risky - individual differences matter far more than birth year.

topics.title: Is profit the only purpose of business?
topics.hook: One classic view says a company's only social responsibility is to increase profits within the rules. The rise of ESG, CSR and 'stakeholder capitalism' challenges that.
topics.why: A foundational management debate that connects strategy, ethics, ESG and India's own mandatory CSR law.
topics.starter: If a company makes huge profits while harming the community around it, has it succeeded? And if it does good but goes bankrupt, has it?
points_for: Profit is the signal that a business is creating value customers will pay for; without it nothing else is sustainable.
Managers are accountable to shareholders who own the company; pursuing other goals with their money is a form of unaccountable power.
Governments, not companies, should set social priorities through laws and taxes.
Profitable firms create jobs, pay taxes and fund innovation - which is itself a social contribution.
points_against: Businesses depend on employees, communities and the environment; ignoring them creates long-term risks to profits too.
Customers, employees and investors increasingly choose companies with purpose and responsible practices.
India already mandates CSR spending for large companies, reflecting a social expectation beyond profit.
Many of the most enduring companies were built around a mission, with profit as a result rather than the sole aim.

topics.title: Family businesses vs professional management - which builds more durable companies?
topics.hook: Most of India's largest business groups are family-run. Some thrive for generations; others stumble in succession battles. Should families step back and hand over to professional managers?
topics.why: Highly relevant for Indian corporate careers, governance and succession planning - and many in this batch will work in or with family businesses.
topics.starter: Family businesses think in generations; professional CEOs often think in quarters. Which mindset actually builds a company that lasts?
points_for: Family ownership brings long-term thinking, patience with investments and a sense of legacy.
Fast decisions without layers of approval can be a real competitive advantage.
Strong values and culture are often preserved better when founders' families stay involved.
Many Indian family groups have successfully combined family ownership with professional executives.
points_against: Succession disputes and family feuds have damaged or split major business groups.
Appointing family members over more capable outsiders can hurt performance and demotivate talented managers.
Weak governance and related-party dealings are bigger risks when ownership and management sit with one family.
Professional management brings fresh skills, accountability and independent boards that investors trust.

topics.title: Should junk-food advertising to children be banned?
topics.hook: Childhood obesity and diabetes are rising in India, while ads for sugary drinks, chips and fast food target children on TV and social media. Should India restrict them?
topics.why: It sits at the intersection of marketing, public health, regulation and corporate responsibility - very relevant for FMCG and marketing roles.
topics.starter: We restrict tobacco and alcohol ads because they harm health. If sugar and junk food are driving a childhood health crisis, why are they different?
points_for: Children can't critically evaluate advertising, especially when it uses cartoons, celebrities and toys.
Rising childhood obesity and early diabetes impose long-term costs on families and the health system.
Restrictions on timing, placement and influencer promotion have been used in other countries to reduce exposure.
It pushes companies to reformulate products with less sugar, salt and fat.
points_against: Parents, not regulators, should decide what children eat; bans can be paternalistic.
Defining 'junk food' is tricky and can unfairly hit traditional snacks and small businesses.
Ads are only one factor; physical activity, school meals and food prices matter as much.
Clear front-of-pack labelling and nutrition education may be more effective than ad bans.

topics.title: Cancel culture - accountability or mob justice?
topics.hook: Brands, celebrities and ordinary people have faced boycotts and social media backlash for remarks or past behaviour. Is this a way for the powerless to hold the powerful accountable - or online mob rule?
topics.why: It tests nuance on free speech, due process, brand reputation and social media - a common GD topic and a real risk for marketing teams.
topics.starter: Twenty years ago, powerful people faced almost no consequences. Today, anyone can lose their job over a tweet. Have we fixed a problem - or created a new one?
points_for: It gives ordinary people a voice to call out harassment, discrimination and abuse that institutions ignored.
Public pressure has pushed companies and institutions to take misconduct seriously.
Consumers boycotting brands is a legitimate use of market power.
It sets clearer social norms about what is acceptable.
points_against: Online outrage often moves faster than facts, punishing people before any investigation.
Punishments can be disproportionate and permanent, with little room for apology or growth.
Fear of backlash discourages open debate and honest discussion.
Campaigns can be weaponised for political or personal agendas rather than accountability.

topics.title: Ladder
topics.hook: A ladder helps you climb - but it has to lean on something, and someone often holds it steady. A rich abstract prompt on growth, hierarchy and support.
topics.why: It lets candidates connect careers, organisations, social mobility and teamwork through one simple image.
topics.starter: A ladder only works if it's leaning on something solid. Maybe the question isn't how fast you climb, but what - and who - you're leaning on.
points_for: Growth: a ladder represents step-by-step progress - every rung matters, and you can't skip too many.
Social mobility: education and jobs act as ladders that lift families out of poverty.
Support: someone holds the ladder - mentors, family, teams - success is rarely solo.
Perspective: the higher you climb, the more you see - leadership is about vision.
points_against: Hierarchy: corporate ladders can encourage politics and competition instead of collaboration.
Pulling up the ladder: people who succeed sometimes block others from following.
Wrong wall: climbing fast is pointless if the ladder is leaning against the wrong goal.
Lattice, not ladder: modern careers move sideways and across, not just up.

topics.title: Bridges vs walls
topics.hook: Bridges connect; walls protect. Both are engineering choices - and both are metaphors for how countries, companies and people relate to each other.
topics.why: A rich topic that can be taken towards trade, immigration, technology, relationships or organisational culture.
topics.starter: Every wall keeps something in and something out. Every bridge lets something across. The real question is: what are we trying to protect, and what are we afraid to connect?
points_for: Bridges: trade, migration and the exchange of ideas have driven most of human progress.
Bridges: cross-functional teams and partnerships break silos and spark innovation.
Bridges: diplomacy and dialogue resolve conflicts more durably than isolation.
Bridges: technology connects people and markets across distances.
points_against: Walls: boundaries protect - privacy, national security, data and personal time all need some walls.
Walls: in trade, some protection helps young domestic industries grow before facing global competition.
Walls: too many bridges without guardrails can spread risks - misinformation, financial contagion, pandemics.
Balance: the best design has bridges with gates - openness with sensible checks.

topics.title: Glass half full, or half empty?
topics.hook: The classic optimism-versus-pessimism question - but strong candidates go further and ask whether the glass is the right size, or who is filling it.
topics.why: It tests whether candidates can avoid clichés and bring fresh, structured angles to a familiar idea.
topics.starter: Optimists say half full, pessimists say half empty. An engineer would say the glass is twice as big as it needs to be. Maybe the smartest answer is to change the question.
points_for: Half full: optimism drives entrepreneurship, resilience and the will to try again after failure.
Half full: focusing on what we have builds gratitude and motivation, and is linked to better wellbeing.
Half full: India's young population and fast growth are reasons for confidence about the future.
Half full: leaders who inspire belief help teams achieve more than they thought possible.
points_against: Half empty: realism helps spot risks early; good risk managers and auditors plan for what's missing.
Half empty: unchecked optimism can lead to overconfidence, bubbles and poor planning.
Reframe: the glass can be refilled - circumstances change with effort and choices.
Reframe: perhaps the glass is the wrong size - question the system, not just the outlook.

topics.title: Clock
topics.hook: A clock measures time but can't create more of it. An abstract topic on time, discipline, urgency and patience.
topics.why: It allows connections to productivity, life choices, ageing populations, climate deadlines and even the GD itself.
topics.starter: Everyone gets the same 24 hours, but nobody gets the same clock. Some people are always early, some always late - and some decide to stop watching the clock altogether.
points_for: Discipline: clocks bring order - deadlines, punctuality and planning make teams and economies work.
Urgency: some problems, like climate change, have a clock ticking - delay has real costs.
Value of time: time is the one resource you can't buy back, so how we spend it matters most.
Cycles: a clock's hands return to the same place - history and business move in cycles too.
points_against: Pressure: obsession with the clock causes stress, burnout and rushed decisions.
Life isn't on one schedule: people succeed at different ages; comparing timelines is unfair.
Patience: some things - trust, expertise, relationships - can't be rushed.
Being present: always watching the clock means missing the moment you're in.

topics.title: Footprints
topics.hook: Footprints show where someone has been - and the mark they leave behind. An abstract topic about legacy, impact and following others.
topics.why: Candidates can take it towards leadership, role models, environmental footprints, digital footprints and personal legacy.
topics.starter: Every step leaves a footprint - in sand, in carbon, online. Some wash away with the next wave; some last for generations. Which kind are we leaving?
points_for: Legacy: leaders and institutions leave footprints for others to follow - mentorship and values outlast careers.
Following footprints: learning from those who came before saves time and avoids mistakes.
Positive impact: every action, however small, can leave a lasting mark on someone's life.
Pioneering: first footprints in new territory - space, science, entrepreneurship - open paths for everyone.
points_against: Carbon footprint: humanity's environmental footprint is harming the planet.
Digital footprint: what we post online stays with us, sometimes harming careers and privacy.
Blindly following: walking only in others' footprints leads nowhere new; innovation needs fresh paths.
Fleeting marks: many footprints vanish quickly - fame and success can be temporary.

topics.title: The butterfly effect
topics.hook: The idea that a butterfly flapping its wings in one place can set off a storm somewhere else - small causes, huge consequences.
topics.why: It rewards candidates who can bring in examples from economics, supply chains, technology and personal choices to show how small actions scale.
topics.starter: One misplaced line of code can crash a global system. One small policy can change millions of lives. Maybe nothing we do is really small.
points_for: Small actions matter: one kind act, one good habit or one well-timed decision can change outcomes dramatically.
Interconnection: global supply chains mean a disruption in one port or factory ripples worldwide.
Innovation: small experiments can scale into industries - many large companies began as side projects.
Policy: small nudges in design, like default options, can shift millions of decisions.
points_against: Unpredictability: the same idea warns us that complex systems can't be fully controlled or forecast.
Unintended consequences: well-meant decisions can backfire far from where they were made.
Overthinking risk: fear of every possible consequence can paralyse action.
Responsibility: if small actions have large effects, so does carelessness - from misinformation to minor safety lapses.
